records.title: Social Engagement Programs of Area Agencies on Aging: Understanding Efforts to Reduce Social Isolation and Loneliness Among Older Adults
records.abstract: Social isolation and loneliness in later life are major public health concerns associated with increased morbidity and premature mortality. Area Agencies on Aging (AAAs) constitute the primary local infrastructure for aging services in the US.  To describe social engagement program types and partnership structures among AAAs and to examine rural–non-rural differences.  We analyzed data from the 2025 National Survey of AAAs (n = 449). Descriptive statistics summarized program and partnership prevalence; item-level Pearson chi-square tests with Bonferroni adjustments compared rural and non-rural agencies.  Most AAAs offered multiple social engagement programs; volunteer engagement (66.0%), arts and creative activities (62.2%), visiting/calling programs (57.7%), and technology engagement (55.5%) were common. Non-rural AAAs were more likely to offer visiting/calling, technology-based activities, and memory cafes, while rural AAAs were more likely to partner with public health units. Rural–non-rural differences suggest context-specific influences of resources and infrastructure on program availability.

records.title: Structural Vulnerability and the Pandemic: Widening Gaps in Nursing Home Antipsychotic Prescribing
records.abstract: To assess whether national reductions in antipsychotic prescribing in U.S. nursing homes were shared equitably or masked widening gaps between top and bottom performers, we examined distributional trends across facilities from 2013 to 2023 using national facility-level data (CMS Provider Data Catalog; LTCFocus). We modeled long-stay antipsychotic measure performance using linear quantile mixed regression, assessed mobility across performance quartiles with transition matrices, and evaluated facility characteristics associated with trajectories. From 2013 to 2019, prescribing fell across all quantiles, with the steepest reductions among the worst performers, narrowing gaps with the best. After 2020, progress diverged: lower-performing facilities experienced sharp setbacks while top performers maintained gains. Mobility analyses showed entrenched disadvantage, with bottom-quartile facilities disproportionately likely to remain there. Higher Medicaid share predicted decline, whereas higher star ratings predicted improvement. The pandemic reversed earlier equity gains, amplifying structural disparities and exposing unequal capacity to sustain improvement.

records.title: Ambivalent return: Older adults’ homecoming after wartime displacement
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
records.abstract: Little is known about how older adults experience their return home after wartime displacement, particularly when home and community are altered or remain insecure. This longitudinal qualitative study examined continuity and change across the displacement–return transition.  Twelve participants (aged 65–92), previously interviewed during displacement (T1), were re-interviewed after returning home (T2) using a qualitative descriptive approach with thematic analysis.  Three themes emerged: (1) the unsettled return, involving altered security, unfamiliarity within the home, and disrupted community life; (2) continuity of social relationships and activities after return; and (3) shifts in life perspective and self-perception. These themes describe the shared dimensions of post-return experience, whereas the complementary diachronic analysis examined how these dimensions changed and combined across T1 and T2. A diachronic analysis identified four return trajectories: functioning but incomplete; ambivalent or gradual return requiring active reorganization; return supported by communal and social continuity and use of personal resources; and ongoing erosion and unresolved damage. Discussion These findings demonstrate that return is not restoration but a reconfiguration of person-environment fit, place identity, belonging, and security in later life. For older adults, this transition involved rebuilding environmental familiarity, security, belonging, and agency rather than simply resuming pre-displacement life. The study highlights social infrastructure as critical for post-return adaptation, underscoring the need for policies recognizing the return process as a significant transition requiring continued communal support.

records.title: Transportation Use, Trip Taking, and Trip Purposes Among Older Adults Not in the Labor Force: Evidence From the 2022 National Household Travel Survey
records.abstract: Transportation needs may differ by labor-force participation status, yet little is known about travel behavior among older adults not in the labor force.  To examine alternative transportation use, trip taking, and trip purposes among older adults not in the labor force.  Data came from the 2022 National Household Travel Survey ( N = 3,474; aged ≥65; not in the labor force). Logistic regression models examined factors associated with transportation mode, taking any trip on the assigned reporting day, and trip purposes.  Nearly 87% drove, 5%–7% used rideshare/taxi, public transit, or bicycles, and one-third walked for transportation. Transportation use and trip-taking varied by socioeconomic characteristics, living arrangements, and digital engagement. Drivers, transportation walkers, and college graduates were more likely to travel. Social/recreational trips were more common among those living alone and among college graduates.  Improving transportation accessibility, affordability, and digital literacy may support late-life mobility and community participation.

records.title: Reducing Stress in Caregivers of People With Dementia in Psychiatric Care: A Proof-of-Concept Evaluation of an Emotion-Focused Group Intervention
records.abstract: Caregivers of people with dementia (CPwD) are at higher risk for psychological stress and mental health issues.  This study evaluated the effectiveness of a brief, four-session group intervention combining socio-medical education, mindfulness and emotion-focused support in reducing stress and improving psychological outcomes in an acute psychiatric hospital setting.  A within-subject waiting-period control design with repeated measures was conducted with N = 52 CPwD. Assessments were performed at baseline, pre-intervention, post-intervention and follow-up. Changes across phases were analyzed using subsequent contrast analyses.  Following the intervention, perceived stress decreased significantly ( p = .038) and general functioning improved ( p = .002) at follow-up. No significant changes were found for depressive symptoms or subjective well-being. The study protocol was designed in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the joint Ethics Committee of the medical faculty at the Ludwig-Maximilians-University of Munich (project number 22-0995).

records.title: Rethinking Behavioral and Psychological Symptoms of Dementia in Severe Alzheimer's Disease: From Intentional Explanation to an Ecological, Body–Environment Framework
records.journal: The International Journal of Aging and Human Development
records.abstract: In contemporary dementia care, behavioral and psychological symptoms of dementia (BPSD) are often understood as expressions of the person's intentions or needs. This paper examines the limits of understanding BPSD as “expressions of intention” in severe Alzheimer's disease. It argues that while desires may still be preserved, the formation and maintenance of beliefs—an essential constituent of intentions in the standard desire–belief model—are likely to be severely compromised. As a result, many behavioral and perceptual symptoms closely related to basic activities of daily living cannot be adequately explained within an intention-based framework. As a complementary framework to existing dementia care theories, this paper proposes a reconceptualization of BPSD as arising from the interaction between embodied procedural memory and environmental affordances. Many BPSD are better understood not as expressions of intention, but as the outcome of situational and non-selective reactivation of fragments of relatively preserved procedural memory in response to the structure of the immediate environment. This reconceptualization extends the focus of care practice beyond the interpretation of the presumed meanings or intentions underlying BPSD and highlights the importance of modifying care environments in ways that appropriately support or constrain the reactivation of procedural memory.

records.title: Development and external validation of a model for predicting family resilience 6 months after stroke in older adults: a prospective cohort study
records.abstract: After stroke, families take long-term responsibility for rehabilitation and care, and family resilience is an important measure of family adaptation. Predicting later family resilience from information collected early during hospitalization may help assess family support needs and plan follow-up care. This study aimed to develop and conduct a preliminary external validation of a model for predicting family resilience 6 months after stroke in older adults.  We used a prospective two-cohort design. The development and independent external validation analyses included 310 and 102 older adults with stroke, respectively. Data were collected at baseline (T0), 1 month (T1), and 6 months after stroke (T2). Using 23 candidate predictors measured early during hospitalization (T0), we developed a least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) linear regression model to predict the continuous score on the shortened Chinese version of the Family Resilience Assessment Scale (FRAS-C) at 6 months (T2). The model was internally validated using repeated nested 10-fold cross-validation and bootstrap resampling, and the final model was applied directly to the independent external cohort. Performance was assessed using the coefficient of determination (R²), root mean square error (RMSE), and calibration measures and compared with the baseline FRAS-C-only model.  The final model included five predictors: baseline family resilience, self-care ability, social support, caregiver sex, and caregiver burden. In repeated nested cross-validation, the model yielded an R² of 0.555 (95% CI 0.499–0.603) and an RMSE of 2.959. In the external validation cohort, the R² was 0.409 (95% CI 0.269–0.508), the RMSE was 3.516, and the calibration slope was 1.165 (95% CI 0.897–1.429). Compared with the baseline FRAS-C-only model, the full model increased R² by 0.238 and reduced RMSE by 0.649 points in external validation.  The model, which included baseline family resilience, patient functional status, and family caregiving characteristics, predicted family resilience at 6 months and added predictive information beyond baseline family resilience alone. It retained predictive performance in the independent external cohort and may be used to support family assessment early during hospitalization and follow-up planning after discharge.

records.title: Perceived Care Among Rural Left-Behind Older Adults in China: A Network Analysis
records.abstract: Rural-to-urban migration separates many rural older adults from adult children and changes how care is received and experienced. Rural left-behind older adults remain in their rural places of origin after family members migrate for work.  This study examined conditional associations among reported care items and compared care networks by number of children and gender.  Cross-sectional data were obtained from 836 rural left-behind older adults aged 55 to 95 who completed the 14-item CSS-RLE. EBIC-LASSO Gaussian graphical models estimated item-level networks, expected influence summarized net signed connectivity, and network comparison tests assessed subgroup differences.  Village care and visits had the highest expected influence in the overall, male, and three-or-more-child networks. Holiday gifts from offspring ranked highest in the one- and two-child networks, whereas living expenses from children ranked highest in the female network. Network structure differed between one-child and larger-family groups and between men and women.

records.title: Understandings of Ageism and Healthcare in the COVID-19 Pandemic
records.journal: The International Journal of Aging and Human Development
records.abstract: Ageism is widespread and intensified during the COVID-19 pandemic, with resource shortages contributing to healthcare guidelines that systematically deprioritised older adults. Whilst the ethical considerations of these guidelines are well documented, perceptions of age and ageism in healthcare allocation remain underexplored. This study examined younger and older adults’ perceptions of age and ageism in healthcare during COVID-19 through a social identity approach. Using a story completion method, 22 older and 41 younger adult participants completed a story about a younger or older COVID-19 patient and doctors allocating the last available ventilator. Using thematic analysis, three themes were developed: (1) age determines health, (2) age determines the value of life, and (3) age determines acceptance of death.  support the need for policies protecting against the influence of ageism in healthcare systems and emphasise the need to understand how internalised ageism may influence perceptions and health behaviours of older patients.

records.title: ‘Keeping me sharp”: Self-perceived effects of grandparenthood on cognition: An exploratory thematic analysis
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
records.abstract: The experience of grandparenthood holds the potential for novel and engaging social interactions and activities, which may protect against cognitive decline. The present study outlines how individuals believe grandparenthood has impacted their cognitive abilities in late life.  We asked 127 grandparents (87 grandmothers and 40 grandfathers) how they thought grandparenthood had impacted their mental ability (memory, concentration, and cognitive ability). An exploratory thematic analysis utilizing a codebook approach was conducted on the participant responses.  Analysis revealed four major themes among the responses: “grandparenthood as a continuous experience that promotes healthy cognitive functioning”, “shifting perspectives”, “limited interaction”, and “the negative impacts of grandparenthood.” Discussion A majority of grandparents expressed the belief that interacting with their grandchildren is beneficial to their cognition. However, some participants qualified grandparenthood as a stressful experience that has negatively impacted their cognitive health. These findings support previous literature showing both cognitive benefits associated with grandparental caregiving and negative cognitive outcomes that may result from the stress of caregiving.

records.title: Social Determinants of Health (SDOH) and Cognition: A Scoping Review
records.abstract: To map the evidence of disparities in cognition across different social determinants of health (SDOH), examine how SDOH are measured in the context of research on cognitive outcomes and identify knowledge gaps. PubMed, the Cochrane Library, and Web of Science were searched. We included peer-reviewed studies of adults that examined SDOH as primary exposures in relation to cognitive outcomes, and described a SDOH framework or definition in the context of cognition. Non-human studies, case reports, case series, editorials, protocols, and -only records were excluded. Ninety-one records were included. Most of the included studies were conducted in the US and the most frequently used framework was the Healthy People (2030) framework. Among studies examining a single SDOH indicator, the Area Deprivation Index (ADI) was the most used measure. Most of the existing research failed to explain the concept of SDOH and lacked a framework to guide the inclusion and interpretation of SDOH indicators. SDOH measures were heterogeneous across studies, with many examining only a single indicator and limited use of multidimensional approaches. This heterogeneity made findings challenging to compare. More research is needed on multidimensional SDOH and cognition in various racial/ethnic groups and less-studied geographic and cultural contexts, under explicit SDOH frameworks.

records.title: Control Beliefs and Emotional Aspects of Psychological Frailty Among Couples in Later Life
records.abstract: This study investigated the associations between control beliefs and the emotional aspects of psychological frailty (i.e., depression, anxiety, and loneliness) among older married couples.  Multivariate Actor-Partner Interdependence Models were used to analyze data from 538 couples aged 65 or older, drawn from the 2022 Health and Retirement Study.  Individuals’ own control beliefs were consistently associated with lower levels of depression, anxiety, and loneliness for both spouses. A partner effect emerged for loneliness, with wives’ control beliefs associated with lower levels of loneliness in their husbands, but this was not significant after adjusting for marital support and strain. Discussion These findings identify control beliefs as a consistent individual-level protective factor. Interventions to improve emotional well-being in older couples should prioritize strengthening personal control beliefs. Dyadic processes merit further investigation, particularly for outcomes such as loneliness that are closely embedded in the relational context.

records.title: Latent Structures of Social Determinants of Health in Later Life: A Comparison of U.S.-Born and Immigrants
records.abstract: This study examined whether the latent structure of social determinants of health (SDOH) differs by nativity and how they relate to health outcomes in later life.  Using 2016–2018 HRS data, exploratory factor analyses by nativity were conducted, followed by nativity-stratified regressions linking SDOH factors to health outcomes.  Four comparable factors emerged in both groups: neighborhood environment, interpersonal stressors, socioeconomic resources, and family support. Loading patterns showed modest nativity differences: among immigrants, social isolation aligned more strongly with family support than socioeconomic resources and perceived discrimination loaded weakly on interpersonal stressors. Interpersonal stressors were associated with poorer mental and cognitive health in both groups; socioeconomic resources were associated with better health outcomes but more weakly among immigrants. Associations of neighborhood environment and family support with health varied by nativity. Discussion Findings indicate substantial commonality in SDOH structures alongside suggestive nativity-related differences, warranting replication in larger immigrant samples.

records.title: Does the Pilot Long-Term Care Insurance Work as Expected in China? Examining its Impact on Hospital Utilizations, Medical Expenses, and Health
records.abstract: This study investigates the impact of long-term care insurance (LTCI) on older adults’ hospital service utilization, medical expenses, and health. Using national representative data from four waves of CHARLS (2011, 2013, 2015, 2018), we find that LTCI decreases older adults’ monthly outpatient visits but is associated with an increase in both annual inpatient stays and inpatient medical expenses. Further evidence suggests that older adults covered by the pilot LTCI program have better health status compared to their counterparts in non-pilot cities. Overall, findings offer empirical support for the role of the LTCI program in Chinese older adults’ hospital service utilization, medical expenses, and health. Findings of China’s LTCI may offer insights for other countries with a large aging population but with no feasible LTCI framework.

records.title: Association Between a Hybrid Video-Guided Multicomponent Exercise Program With Staff Assistance and Free-Living Gait in Older Adults With Knee and Low Back Pain: Secondary Analysis of a Randomized Controlled Trial
records.abstract: Older adults with chronic joint pain often exhibit decreased mobility. Daily walking measures are being increasingly used in aging research as  indicators of mobility.  In this study, we aimed to examine the effects of a 12-week hybrid exercise-based program on daily-life walking characteristics.  A total of 59 community-dwelling older adults (aged ≥65 years) with mild to moderate knee and/or low back pain were randomized to either a hybrid exercise group or an educational control group. Daily-life walking was monitored using an ankle sensor. Daily observation data were collected within 2 planned 7-day windows. Primary parameters included activity volume and gait characteristics. Statistical analyses were conducted based on a modified intention-to-treat principle using linear mixed-effects models, with a per-protocol set used for sensitivity analyses.  The mixed-effects analysis based on the modified intention-to-treat principle (n=52 participants; 696 observations) suggested an effect of the intervention on improving walking quality, particularly step length (β=2.39 cm; P =.04; Hedges g =0.493), with a smaller effect with borderline statistical significance observed on improving walking speed (β=0.05 m/s; P =.06; Hedges g =0.496). Cadence, daily distance, daily steps, active energy expenditure, and accumulated 3 or more metabolic equivalent of task activities showed no clear difference between the groups. In the per-protocol sensitivity analysis (n=44), the same directional pattern of improvement was observed for step length (β=1.95 cm; P =.13; Hedges g =0.365) and walking speed (β=0.04 m/s; P =.14; Hedges g =0.368); however, the estimates were imprecise.  A 12-week hybrid exercise program may improve the quality of daily-life walking, with the clearest effect observed on step length. Given the attenuation after multiplicity-aware interpretation and in sensitivity analyses, these findings should be interpreted as suggestive rather than definitive.

records.title: Deprescribing Fall Risk–Increasing Drugs in Older Adults: Implementation Challenges and a Conceptual Framework from the DeFRID Trial and Global Evidence
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
records.abstract: Deprescribing fall risk–increasing drugs (FRIDs) is essential for reducing polypharmacy and falls in older adults, yet randomized controlled trials (RCTs) face unique implementation challenges. The DeFRID study is an ongoing multi-center RCT evaluating an ARMOR-based deprescribing intervention versus usual care in adults aged ≥60 years prescribed FRIDs. The  of this review are threefold: (1) to describe practical challenges encountered during a multi-center deprescribing RCT in India; (2) to propose a conceptual framework for categorizing these barriers; and (3) to contextualize DeFRID's experience within the broader deprescribing research landscape.  We conducted a narrative review with systematic scoping elements, synthesizing global RCT evidence from PubMed, OpenAlex, and Google Scholar (inception–December 2025) with DeFRID process evaluation data. DeFRID barriers and facilitators were identified via mixed- (clinician KAP questionnaire and qualitative interviews), team meetings, retention logs, and Phase II RCT implementation data, thematically categorized, then compared with global RCT challenges.  DeFRID implementation revealed four challenge categories: ethical–clinical difficulties establishing equipoise for FRID withdrawal; operational barriers to recruitment and retention; methodological complexities in fall outcome ascertainment; and context-specific constraints unique to the Indian LMIC setting—limited deprescribing guidelines, polypharmacy normalization, fragmented care coordination, and hierarchical decision-making. Global RCTs revealed substantial implementation challenges: low clinician adherence, short follow-up periods, restrictive eligibility excluding frail or cognitively impaired older adults, and resource-intensive interventions limiting scalability.  Deprescribing FRIDs in older adults is impeded by ethical, operational, methodological, and provider-patient challenges, necessitating multilevel strategies integrating training, shared decision-making, context-specific guidelines, and stakeholder engagement for scalable implementation.

records.title: Sustaining agency after a fall: navigating healthcare and adjusting everyday life – a qualitative interview study
records.abstract: Falls among older adults are a major public health concern and are associated with recurrent falls, functional decline, fear of falling, and reduced quality of life. Older adults presenting to emergency departments (EDs) following a fall are often discharged directly home despite ongoing rehabilitation and support needs. Although person-centred approaches are recommended in international guidelines, less is known about older adults’ and relatives’ experiences following an ED visit for a fall. This study aimed to describe older adults’ and their relatives’ experiences of a fall, including the ED visit and the transition back home. Method A qualitative study design was used, involving semi-structured interviews with older adults aged 75 years and older and their relatives. Participants had attended the ED following a fall but were discharged without hospital admission. Seventeen participants (11 older adults and 6 relatives) were recruited. Data were analysed using qualitative content analysis according to Graneheim and Lundman.  The analysis generated one overarching theme, Sustaining agency through recovery across care and everyday life , which reflected how older adults and their relatives sought to manage daily life following a fall. Both groups described addressing immediate care needs while simultaneously adapting to longer-term changes in everyday life. Participants described difficulties navigating healthcare services to access follow-up care and rehabilitation, contributing to feelings of insecurity, financial strain, and increased responsibility. A persistent fear of falling affected daily activities and required adaptations and new roles for both older adults and their relatives. Despite these challenges, many participants demonstrated resilience and an ability to manage daily life following injury. Individual coping strategies and support from relatives were described as central to managing everyday life and healthcare contacts.  Older adults discharged home after a fall may benefit from coordinated, person-centred follow- up that supports rehabilitation, recovery, and fall prevention. Despite variation in support needs, participants described a common need for clearer guidance and improved support structures, while also demonstrating considerable resilience and capacity for self-management. records.title: Socioeconomic Differences in the Association Between the Big Five Personality Traits and Episodic Memory Trajectories in Midlife and Old Age
records.abstract: : Episodic memory trajectories vary substantially between individuals in the second half of life: some maintain high levels of performance into their 80s, whereas others experience marked declines as early as their 50s. Identifying factors that help explain this heterogeneity is critical for understanding cognitive aging. Drawing on the resource substitution hypothesis and the Openness–Fluid–Crystallized–Intelligence (OFCI) model, this preregistered study examined whether the Big Five personality traits and their interactions with socioeconomic status (SES) predict individual differences in episodic memory trajectories, testing also potential non-linear associations. We expected higher openness and lower neuroticism to be associated with better memory levels and slower decline, with stronger effects at lower levels of SES. : We analyzed data from 57,947 individuals aged 50 and older (M = 67.78, SD = 9.03) who participated in at least two waves (7, 8, or 9) of the Survey of Health, Ageing, and Retirement in Europe (SHARE). Multilevel growth models were used to estimate associations between personality and episodic memory levels and 5-year change, and whether SES (i.e., education, income, and wealth) moderated these associations. : Consistent with the OFCI model and the resource substitution hypothesis, higher openness was associated with better episodic memory levels, particularly among individuals with lower wealth. Higher neuroticism and lower conscientiousness were linked to poorer episodic memory levels, but only among less wealthy individuals. Higher extraversion was associated with better memory levels overall, and individuals at the extremes of extraversion exhibited somewhat flatter declines compared to those with moderate levels. Except for extraversion, there was little evidence for non-linear associations or for associations with 5-year change in episodic memory. : Our findings underscore the relevance of wealth as an important socioeconomic resource for cognitive health beyond income and education, particularly in old age, when income is typically reduced. Overall, the  support modest concurrent associations between personality, SES, and episodic memory levels, but provide hardly any evidence for longitudinal effects. More frequent and longer-term longitudinal assessments are needed to clarify potential effects on cognitive aging.

records.title: Large Language Model–Based Identification of Subjective Cognitive Decline in Electronic Health Records Among Older Adults With Normal Cognitive Testing: Retrospective Cohort Study
records.abstract: Subjective cognitive decline (SCD) typically refers to self- or informant-reported decline in cognition despite the absence of  impairment on standardized testing. Older adults with documented normal cognitive test performance provide a pragmatic anchor cohort for electronic health record (EHR)–based SCD phenotyping. However, cognitive concerns are primarily recorded in unstructured notes and are inconsistently documented, making it unclear how often and in whom concerns are captured in routine care.  This study aims to operationalize EHR-based SCD phenotyping in an objectively normal-testing cohort using a large language model (LLM)–based natural language processing approach and to examine the frequency and clinical and sociodemographic correlates of cognitive concern documentation.  We conducted an EHR-based observational study of patients aged 65 years or older with a first normal cognitive test recorded in EHR flowsheets between January 2019 and April 2024 in a large health care system. We developed and iteratively refined a 2-stage LLM-based natural language processing pipeline to identify documented cognitive concerns in unstructured notes during the 12 months prior to the index date, and evaluated performance against manual review. We quantified the frequency of documented concerns within this normal-testing cohort and used multivariable logistic regression to assess associations with sociodemographic factors (age, marital status, insurance, and neighborhood Area Deprivation Index), sequentially adjusting for clinical comorbidities and relevant medications.  Among 15,750 older adults with normal cognitive test scores, 13.8% (n=2175) had at least 1 documented cognitive concern in the prior year, captured in 1.2% (7394/605,177) of notes. On manual validation, the 2-stage pipeline (Med42-v2-8B screening followed by GPT-4o confirmation) achieved a sensitivity of 0.957, positive predictive value of 0.935, specificity of 0.985, and F 1 -score of 0.945 for cognitive concern identification. Documentation was more likely in older individuals, those with commercial (vs Medicare) insurance, and those with neurological and psychiatric conditions. In fully adjusted models, Parkinson disease (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 5.29, 95% CI 3.60‐7.77), traumatic brain injury (aOR 4.63, 95% CI 3.15‐6.81), stroke or transient ischemic attack (aOR 3.46, 95% CI 3.15‐4.18), epilepsy (aOR 2.52, 95% CI 1.83‐3.49), depression (aOR 1.54, 95% CI 1.36‐1.75), and excessive alcohol use (aOR 1.48, 95% CI 1.06‐2.06) were among the strongest correlates of cognitive concern documentation. In contrast, obesity (aOR 0.73, 95% CI 0.65‐0.82), hyperlipidemia (aOR 0.59, 95% CI 0.51‐0.67), and residence in more deprived neighborhoods (higher Area Deprivation Index) were associated with lower odds of documented cognitive concerns. Documentation was uncommon and selectively captured by clinical and sociodemographic factors, with implications for equity and the validity of EHR-based phenotypes.

records.title: Blind giving predicts longitudinal increases in scam susceptibility in later life
records.abstract: and  Financial fraud is a common and consequential threat among older adults, with estimated prevalence rates ranging from 4% to 17% annually. Although cognitive decline has been widely studied as a risk factor, less is known about behavioral characteristics that may predict changes in scam susceptibility. In the present study, we examined whether blind giving predicted trajectories of scam susceptibility across a two-year period and whether this association differed as a function of age. Research Design and  One hundred and sixteen cognitively unimpaired older adults (aged 51 to 83; 72% female) completed a behavioral economic measure of blind giving at baseline and a self-report measure of scam susceptibility annually across three visits.  Linear mixed-effects models revealed a significant interaction between time, blind giving, and age (p = .022), such that greater baseline blind giving was associated with increasing scam susceptibility over time among relatively older participants, whereas scam susceptibility remained stable across levels of blind giving among relatively younger participants. Blind giving was not associated with scam susceptibility at baseline (p = .515), and the longitudinal association persisted after separately adjusting for global cognition, socioeconomic status, and race (all ps ≤ .026).  Greater blind giving predicted longitudinal increases in scam susceptibility over a two-year period, with this pattern observed specifically in advanced age. These findings suggest that prosocial tendencies may become maladaptive in later life, underscoring the importance of identifying at-risk individuals to inform prevention efforts in aging populations.

records.title: Being Sensed, Scored, and ‘Connected’: A Social-Gerontological Critique of AI-Driven Loneliness Detection for Older Adults in Taiwan
records.abstract: Enthusiasm for artificial intelligence (AI) that continuously infers emotion promises to change how care systems identify older adults at risk of loneliness. We use AI-driven loneliness detection to mean systems that infer loneliness, or a proxy for it, from sensed data rather than from a person’s answer, rendering the inference as a score or category used in care; they range from facial and vocal emotion recognition to behavioral risk prediction from everyday activity data. Engineering feasibility, more than any social-gerontological understanding of loneliness, has driven this agenda, and little attention has gone to how older adults in different cultural contexts wish to be known and supported. Because such detection is not yet in routine use in Taiwan, this Forum article adopts an anticipatory-governance stance, examining before deployment a trajectory that policy makes plausible. Anchored in Taiwan’s ageing society and long-term care system, it argues that culturally responsive design should begin with older adults’ own meanings, relational obligations, and expectations of privacy and autonomy, not with the sensors. It identifies three tensions for social gerontology: the reframing of a relational experience as an individual biometric deficit; the risk that algorithms read culturally patterned emotional restraint as noise; and the slippage from care toward surveillance once risk indices enter routine care workflows. Taking seriously the case for technological augmentation of scarce care resources, the article proposes principles for a socially accountable approach and a research agenda on how older adults negotiate being sensed, scored, and ‘connected.’

records.title: Vulnerability Intersections: An Integrative Conceptual Framework for Understanding Vulnerability in AI-Assisted Care for Older Adults
records.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) applications are increasingly used to support independent living and care for older adults, particularly those in vulnerable situations. Yet, how vulnerability is constructed when AI enters later-life care remains poorly theorized. Existing approaches to vulnerability in old age inadequately address AI-related risks, structural conditions, exposure pathways, and life course disadvantages. Using a theory-synthesis approach, this article proposes “vulnerability intersections” as an integrative framework for how vulnerability is constructed, enacted, and negotiated in AI-assisted care for older adults. The framework extends existing sociotechnical accounts by conceptualizing vulnerability as taking four overlapping forms: anticipatory, opaque, routinized, and normative. It locates vulnerability factors at the micro level of older adults’ lives, the meso level of care organizations and technology providers, and the macro level of political-economic and regulatory arrangements, with life-course accumulation spanning all three. It also proposes three exposure pathways through which vulnerability factors become consequential: AI-mediated information and representations of aging; AI-powered care organization and delivery; and AI-configured power, participation, and social relations. The framework shifts attention away from viewing older adults as inherently vulnerable toward examining the sociotechnical arrangements under which vulnerability is anticipated, classified, distributed, and negotiated when AI enters care.

records.title: Functional status and depressive symptoms in relation to bone mineral density and osteoporosis in hospitalized older adults: a cross-sectional study
records.abstract: Introduction Osteoporosis is a major cause of morbidity and fractures among older adults, contributing substantially to disability, hospitalization, and mortality. This cross-sectional study investigated the associations of depressive symptoms and functional status with bone mineral density (BMD) and osteoporosis in hospitalized older adults.  We analyzed 1,048 hospitalized patients aged ≥ 70 years who underwent dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA). Depressive symptoms (GDS-15) and functional status (Barthel Index) were extracted from routine geriatric assessments. Group comparisons, multivariable linear regression, and logistic regression analyses were performed after adjustment for demographic, clinical, and endocrine covariates.  Lower Barthel Index scores and higher depressive symptom burden were independently associated with lower hip BMD, whereas associations with lumbar spine BMD were less consistent. Although statistically significant, the observed effect sizes were modest. The multivariable model explained a moderate proportion of BMD variability (adjusted R² = 0.22).  Functional and psychological characteristics were independently associated with bone mineral density in hospitalized older adults. Given the cross-sectional design, causal relationships cannot be established. These findings support the potential value of incorporating comprehensive geriatric assessment into osteoporosis evaluation to improve identification of older adults at increased fracture risk.

records.title: Components of family empowerment for family caregivers of older adults with dementia: focus group interviews
records.abstract: Strengthening empowerment plays a pivotal role in supporting family caregivers of older adults with dementia. This study explored the comprehensive caregiving experiences of both family caregivers and dementia care professionals to identify and describe the components of family empowerment within the Korean context.  A qualitative study was conducted using semi-structured focus group interviews (FGIs). Participants included 14 family caregivers (3 groups) and 5 Dementia care professionals (1 group). Psychological Empowerment Model (PEM) served as the theoretical framework to understand the dimensions of empowerment. The specific components of empowerment in Korean family caregivers of older adults with dementia were analyzed using qualitative thematic analysis.  Seven main themes and 14 sub-themes were identified as components of family empowerment. The main themes included: (1) Reconstructing the caregiving situation and awareness; (2) Acquiring dementia information through experiential means; (3) Satisfaction with doing my best in caregiving; (4) Balance between self-care and family care; (5) Securing and utilizing dementia-related resources; (6) Reflections of caregiving experiences; and (7) New roles and relationships created through caregiving.  The findings of the study elucidate that family empowerment of family caregivers of older adults with dementia is a multidimensional construct: it is established through the cognitive process of reconstructing caregiving perceptions, emotional fulfillment derived from the stability of the caregiving process, behavioral practices of balancing self-care with family care, and relational reinforcement gained through newly established roles. Future efforts should establish sustainable support systems through education, resource linkage, and emotional support. Additionally, we propose the development of empowerment intervention programs and measurement tools based on these identified components. Clinical trial number Not applicable.

records.title: Associations of Midlife Gait Speed and Muscle Performance With Falls in Later Life: Secondary Analysis of the MIDUS Cohort
records.abstract: Falls are a major cause of morbidity among older adults, yet fall risk may begin to emerge during midlife. Physical performance measures may identify early functional vulnerability associated with later-life health outcomes.  This study examined whether midlife gait speed and muscle performance were associated with recurrent falls later in life.  This study was a secondary analysis of prospectively collected data from the Midlife in the United States (MIDUS) cohort. Independent adults (n=309) aged 45 to 64 years at wave 2 (2004-2009) who completed physical performance assessments were followed to wave 3 (2013-2021). Baseline measures included gait speed from a 50-foot walk test, grip strength, sit-to-stand time, and calculated lower-extremity power. The primary analysis examined associations between baseline physical performance and recurrent falls at follow-up (≥2 falls in the previous 12 months). A sensitivity analysis repeated the primary models but was restricted to participants without a baseline history of recurrent falls.  At follow-up, 20.4% (63/309) of participants reported recurrent falls. Slower midlife gait speed was associated with higher odds of recurrent falls (odds ratio 1.43, 95% CI 1.05-1.95; P=.02), whereas muscle performance measures were not associated with falls in the primary analysis. The association between slower gait speed and recurrent falls remained significant in the sensitivity analysis. Over follow-up, muscle performance declined, whereas gait speed remained stable.  Slower midlife gait speed was associated with higher odds of recurrent falls, suggesting that fall vulnerability may be detectable as early as midlife. Given the exploratory nature of this study, further studies are warranted to confirm these findings.

records.title: Planetary Health Diet Adherence and Frailty in Older Adults: Evidence from the Seniors-ENRICA Cohorts
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
records.abstract: Frailty is a major determinant of disability and adverse outcomes in older adults. The Planetary Health Diet (PHD), a plant-based dietary pattern promoting environmental sustainability, has been associated with lower mortality and reduced chronic disease risk. We examined the association between adherence to the Planetary Health Diet Index (PHDI) and frailty over time using repeated frailty assessments.  Data came from two cohorts of community-dwelling older adults: Seniors-ENRICA-1 (2008-2015; ≥60 years; n = 3,289) and Seniors-ENRICA-2 (2015-2023; ≥65 years; n = 3,273). Baseline diet was assessed using a validated diet history, and adherence to the PHD was assessed using the PHDI (0-140), based on 15 food groups. Frailty was defined by the Fried phenotype (≥3 criteria of exhaustion, low physical activity, slow gait, muscle weakness, unintentional weight loss). Generalized estimating equation (GEE) models estimated odds ratios (OR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) for frailty across PHDI tertiles, adjusting for sociodemographic, lifestyle, and clinical factors.  Higher PHDI adherence was consistently associated with lower odds of frailty over time. Comparing highest vs. lowest tertiles, multivariable-adjusted ORs (95% CI) were 0.62 (0.42, 0.92) in Seniors-ENRICA-1, 0.40 (0.24, 0.65) in Seniors-ENRICA-2 and 0.52 (0.38, 0.70) in the pooled analyses. Higher PHDI adherence was primarily associated with lower odds of low physical activity, while vegetables and fruits showed the strongest independent associations among individual PHDI components.  Greater PHDI adherence is associated with lower odds of frailty in Spanish older adults, supporting the potential role of sustainable, plant-based dietary patterns for healthy ageing.

featuredDrafts.title: Social Engagement Programs of Area Agencies on Aging: Understanding Efforts to Reduce Social Isolation and Loneliness Among Older Adults
featuredDrafts.abstract: Social isolation and loneliness in later life are major public health concerns associated with increased morbidity and premature mortality. Area Agencies on Aging (AAAs) constitute the primary local infrastructure for aging services in the US.  To describe social engagement program types and partnership structures among AAAs and to examine rural–non-rural differences.  We analyzed data from the 2025 National Survey of AAAs (n = 449). Descriptive statistics summarized program and partnership prevalence; item-level Pearson chi-square tests with Bonferroni adjustments compared rural and non-rural agencies.  Most AAAs offered multiple social engagement programs; volunteer engagement (66.0%), arts and creative activities (62.2%), visiting/calling programs (57.7%), and technology engagement (55.5%) were common. Non-rural AAAs were more likely to offer visiting/calling, technology-based activities, and memory cafes, while rural AAAs were more likely to partner with public health units. Rural–non-rural differences suggest context-specific influences of resources and infrastructure on program availability.

featuredDrafts.title: Structural Vulnerability and the Pandemic: Widening Gaps in Nursing Home Antipsychotic Prescribing
featuredDrafts.abstract: To assess whether national reductions in antipsychotic prescribing in U.S. nursing homes were shared equitably or masked widening gaps between top and bottom performers, we examined distributional trends across facilities from 2013 to 2023 using national facility-level data (CMS Provider Data Catalog; LTCFocus). We modeled long-stay antipsychotic measure performance using linear quantile mixed regression, assessed mobility across performance quartiles with transition matrices, and evaluated facility characteristics associated with trajectories. From 2013 to 2019, prescribing fell across all quantiles, with the steepest reductions among the worst performers, narrowing gaps with the best. After 2020, progress diverged: lower-performing facilities experienced sharp setbacks while top performers maintained gains. Mobility analyses showed entrenched disadvantage, with bottom-quartile facilities disproportionately likely to remain there. Higher Medicaid share predicted decline, whereas higher star ratings predicted improvement. The pandemic reversed earlier equity gains, amplifying structural disparities and exposing unequal capacity to sustain improvement.

featuredDrafts.title: Ambivalent return: Older adults’ homecoming after wartime displacement
featuredDrafts.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
featuredDrafts.abstract: Little is known about how older adults experience their return home after wartime displacement, particularly when home and community are altered or remain insecure. This longitudinal qualitative study examined continuity and change across the displacement–return transition.  Twelve participants (aged 65–92), previously interviewed during displacement (T1), were re-interviewed after returning home (T2) using a qualitative descriptive approach with thematic analysis.  Three themes emerged: (1) the unsettled return, involving altered security, unfamiliarity within the home, and disrupted community life; (2) continuity of social relationships and activities after return; and (3) shifts in life perspective and self-perception. These themes describe the shared dimensions of post-return experience, whereas the complementary diachronic analysis examined how these dimensions changed and combined across T1 and T2. A diachronic analysis identified four return trajectories: functioning but incomplete; ambivalent or gradual return requiring active reorganization; return supported by communal and social continuity and use of personal resources; and ongoing erosion and unresolved damage. Discussion These findings demonstrate that return is not restoration but a reconfiguration of person-environment fit, place identity, belonging, and security in later life. For older adults, this transition involved rebuilding environmental familiarity, security, belonging, and agency rather than simply resuming pre-displacement life. The study highlights social infrastructure as critical for post-return adaptation, underscoring the need for policies recognizing the return process as a significant transition requiring continued communal support.

featuredDrafts.title: Transportation Use, Trip Taking, and Trip Purposes Among Older Adults Not in the Labor Force: Evidence From the 2022 National Household Travel Survey
featuredDrafts.abstract: Transportation needs may differ by labor-force participation status, yet little is known about travel behavior among older adults not in the labor force.  To examine alternative transportation use, trip taking, and trip purposes among older adults not in the labor force.  Data came from the 2022 National Household Travel Survey ( N = 3,474; aged ≥65; not in the labor force). Logistic regression models examined factors associated with transportation mode, taking any trip on the assigned reporting day, and trip purposes.  Nearly 87% drove, 5%–7% used rideshare/taxi, public transit, or bicycles, and one-third walked for transportation. Transportation use and trip-taking varied by socioeconomic characteristics, living arrangements, and digital engagement. Drivers, transportation walkers, and college graduates were more likely to travel. Social/recreational trips were more common among those living alone and among college graduates.  Improving transportation accessibility, affordability, and digital literacy may support late-life mobility and community participation.

featuredDrafts.title: Reducing Stress in Caregivers of People With Dementia in Psychiatric Care: A Proof-of-Concept Evaluation of an Emotion-Focused Group Intervention
featuredDrafts.abstract: Caregivers of people with dementia (CPwD) are at higher risk for psychological stress and mental health issues.  This study evaluated the effectiveness of a brief, four-session group intervention combining socio-medical education, mindfulness and emotion-focused support in reducing stress and improving psychological outcomes in an acute psychiatric hospital setting.  A within-subject waiting-period control design with repeated measures was conducted with N = 52 CPwD. Assessments were performed at baseline, pre-intervention, post-intervention and follow-up. Changes across phases were analyzed using subsequent contrast analyses.  Following the intervention, perceived stress decreased significantly ( p = .038) and general functioning improved ( p = .002) at follow-up. No significant changes were found for depressive symptoms or subjective well-being. The study protocol was designed in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the joint Ethics Committee of the medical faculty at the Ludwig-Maximilians-University of Munich (project number 22-0995).

featuredDrafts.title: Rethinking Behavioral and Psychological Symptoms of Dementia in Severe Alzheimer's Disease: From Intentional Explanation to an Ecological, Body–Environment Framework
featuredDrafts.journal: The International Journal of Aging and Human Development
featuredDrafts.abstract: In contemporary dementia care, behavioral and psychological symptoms of dementia (BPSD) are often understood as expressions of the person's intentions or needs. This paper examines the limits of understanding BPSD as “expressions of intention” in severe Alzheimer's disease. It argues that while desires may still be preserved, the formation and maintenance of beliefs—an essential constituent of intentions in the standard desire–belief model—are likely to be severely compromised. As a result, many behavioral and perceptual symptoms closely related to basic activities of daily living cannot be adequately explained within an intention-based framework. As a complementary framework to existing dementia care theories, this paper proposes a reconceptualization of BPSD as arising from the interaction between embodied procedural memory and environmental affordances. Many BPSD are better understood not as expressions of intention, but as the outcome of situational and non-selective reactivation of fragments of relatively preserved procedural memory in response to the structure of the immediate environment. This reconceptualization extends the focus of care practice beyond the interpretation of the presumed meanings or intentions underlying BPSD and highlights the importance of modifying care environments in ways that appropriately support or constrain the reactivation of procedural memory.

featuredDrafts.title: Development and external validation of a model for predicting family resilience 6 months after stroke in older adults: a prospective cohort study
featuredDrafts.abstract: After stroke, families take long-term responsibility for rehabilitation and care, and family resilience is an important measure of family adaptation. Predicting later family resilience from information collected early during hospitalization may help assess family support needs and plan follow-up care. This study aimed to develop and conduct a preliminary external validation of a model for predicting family resilience 6 months after stroke in older adults.  We used a prospective two-cohort design. The development and independent external validation analyses included 310 and 102 older adults with stroke, respectively. Data were collected at baseline (T0), 1 month (T1), and 6 months after stroke (T2). Using 23 candidate predictors measured early during hospitalization (T0), we developed a least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) linear regression model to predict the continuous score on the shortened Chinese version of the Family Resilience Assessment Scale (FRAS-C) at 6 months (T2). The model was internally validated using repeated nested 10-fold cross-validation and bootstrap resampling, and the final model was applied directly to the independent external cohort. Performance was assessed using the coefficient of determination (R²), root mean square error (RMSE), and calibration measures and compared with the baseline FRAS-C-only model.  The final model included five predictors: baseline family resilience, self-care ability, social support, caregiver sex, and caregiver burden. In repeated nested cross-validation, the model yielded an R² of 0.555 (95% CI 0.499–0.603) and an RMSE of 2.959. In the external validation cohort, the R² was 0.409 (95% CI 0.269–0.508), the RMSE was 3.516, and the calibration slope was 1.165 (95% CI 0.897–1.429). Compared with the baseline FRAS-C-only model, the full model increased R² by 0.238 and reduced RMSE by 0.649 points in external validation.  The model, which included baseline family resilience, patient functional status, and family caregiving characteristics, predicted family resilience at 6 months and added predictive information beyond baseline family resilience alone. It retained predictive performance in the independent external cohort and may be used to support family assessment early during hospitalization and follow-up planning after discharge.

featuredDrafts.title: Perceived Care Among Rural Left-Behind Older Adults in China: A Network Analysis
featuredDrafts.abstract: Rural-to-urban migration separates many rural older adults from adult children and changes how care is received and experienced. Rural left-behind older adults remain in their rural places of origin after family members migrate for work.  This study examined conditional associations among reported care items and compared care networks by number of children and gender.  Cross-sectional data were obtained from 836 rural left-behind older adults aged 55 to 95 who completed the 14-item CSS-RLE. EBIC-LASSO Gaussian graphical models estimated item-level networks, expected influence summarized net signed connectivity, and network comparison tests assessed subgroup differences.  Village care and visits had the highest expected influence in the overall, male, and three-or-more-child networks. Holiday gifts from offspring ranked highest in the one- and two-child networks, whereas living expenses from children ranked highest in the female network. Network structure differed between one-child and larger-family groups and between men and women.

featuredDrafts.journal: The International Journal of Aging and Human Development
featuredDrafts.abstract: Ageism is widespread and intensified during the COVID-19 pandemic, with resource shortages contributing to healthcare guidelines that systematically deprioritised older adults. Whilst the ethical considerations of these guidelines are well documented, perceptions of age and ageism in healthcare allocation remain underexplored. This study examined younger and older adults’ perceptions of age and ageism in healthcare during COVID-19 through a social identity approach. Using a story completion method, 22 older and 41 younger adult participants completed a story about a younger or older COVID-19 patient and doctors allocating the last available ventilator. Using thematic analysis, three themes were developed: (1) age determines health, (2) age determines the value of life, and (3) age determines acceptance of death.  support the need for policies protecting against the influence of ageism in healthcare systems and emphasise the need to understand how internalised ageism may influence perceptions and health behaviours of older patients.

featuredDrafts.title: ‘Keeping me sharp”: Self-perceived effects of grandparenthood on cognition: An exploratory thematic analysis
featuredDrafts.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
featuredDrafts.abstract: The experience of grandparenthood holds the potential for novel and engaging social interactions and activities, which may protect against cognitive decline. The present study outlines how individuals believe grandparenthood has impacted their cognitive abilities in late life.  We asked 127 grandparents (87 grandmothers and 40 grandfathers) how they thought grandparenthood had impacted their mental ability (memory, concentration, and cognitive ability). An exploratory thematic analysis utilizing a codebook approach was conducted on the participant responses.  Analysis revealed four major themes among the responses: “grandparenthood as a continuous experience that promotes healthy cognitive functioning”, “shifting perspectives”, “limited interaction”, and “the negative impacts of grandparenthood.” Discussion A majority of grandparents expressed the belief that interacting with their grandchildren is beneficial to their cognition. However, some participants qualified grandparenthood as a stressful experience that has negatively impacted their cognitive health. These findings support previous literature showing both cognitive benefits associated with grandparental caregiving and negative cognitive outcomes that may result from the stress of caregiving.

featuredDrafts.title: Social Determinants of Health (SDOH) and Cognition: A Scoping Review
featuredDrafts.abstract: To map the evidence of disparities in cognition across different social determinants of health (SDOH), examine how SDOH are measured in the context of research on cognitive outcomes and identify knowledge gaps. PubMed, the Cochrane Library, and Web of Science were searched. We included peer-reviewed studies of adults that examined SDOH as primary exposures in relation to cognitive outcomes, and described a SDOH framework or definition in the context of cognition. Non-human studies, case reports, case series, editorials, protocols, and -only records were excluded. Ninety-one records were included. Most of the included studies were conducted in the US and the most frequently used framework was the Healthy People (2030) framework. Among studies examining a single SDOH indicator, the Area Deprivation Index (ADI) was the most used measure. Most of the existing research failed to explain the concept of SDOH and lacked a framework to guide the inclusion and interpretation of SDOH indicators. SDOH measures were heterogeneous across studies, with many examining only a single indicator and limited use of multidimensional approaches. This heterogeneity made findings challenging to compare. More research is needed on multidimensional SDOH and cognition in various racial/ethnic groups and less-studied geographic and cultural contexts, under explicit SDOH frameworks.

featuredDrafts.title: Control Beliefs and Emotional Aspects of Psychological Frailty Among Couples in Later Life
featuredDrafts.abstract: This study investigated the associations between control beliefs and the emotional aspects of psychological frailty (i.e., depression, anxiety, and loneliness) among older married couples.  Multivariate Actor-Partner Interdependence Models were used to analyze data from 538 couples aged 65 or older, drawn from the 2022 Health and Retirement Study.  Individuals’ own control beliefs were consistently associated with lower levels of depression, anxiety, and loneliness for both spouses. A partner effect emerged for loneliness, with wives’ control beliefs associated with lower levels of loneliness in their husbands, but this was not significant after adjusting for marital support and strain. Discussion These findings identify control beliefs as a consistent individual-level protective factor. Interventions to improve emotional well-being in older couples should prioritize strengthening personal control beliefs. Dyadic processes merit further investigation, particularly for outcomes such as loneliness that are closely embedded in the relational context.

featuredDrafts.title: Latent Structures of Social Determinants of Health in Later Life: A Comparison of U.S.-Born and Immigrants
featuredDrafts.abstract: This study examined whether the latent structure of social determinants of health (SDOH) differs by nativity and how they relate to health outcomes in later life.  Using 2016–2018 HRS data, exploratory factor analyses by nativity were conducted, followed by nativity-stratified regressions linking SDOH factors to health outcomes.  Four comparable factors emerged in both groups: neighborhood environment, interpersonal stressors, socioeconomic resources, and family support. Loading patterns showed modest nativity differences: among immigrants, social isolation aligned more strongly with family support than socioeconomic resources and perceived discrimination loaded weakly on interpersonal stressors. Interpersonal stressors were associated with poorer mental and cognitive health in both groups; socioeconomic resources were associated with better health outcomes but more weakly among immigrants. Associations of neighborhood environment and family support with health varied by nativity. Discussion Findings indicate substantial commonality in SDOH structures alongside suggestive nativity-related differences, warranting replication in larger immigrant samples.

featuredDrafts.title: Does the Pilot Long-Term Care Insurance Work as Expected in China? Examining its Impact on Hospital Utilizations, Medical Expenses, and Health
featuredDrafts.abstract: This study investigates the impact of long-term care insurance (LTCI) on older adults’ hospital service utilization, medical expenses, and health. Using national representative data from four waves of CHARLS (2011, 2013, 2015, 2018), we find that LTCI decreases older adults’ monthly outpatient visits but is associated with an increase in both annual inpatient stays and inpatient medical expenses. Further evidence suggests that older adults covered by the pilot LTCI program have better health status compared to their counterparts in non-pilot cities. Overall, findings offer empirical support for the role of the LTCI program in Chinese older adults’ hospital service utilization, medical expenses, and health. Findings of China’s LTCI may offer insights for other countries with a large aging population but with no feasible LTCI framework.

featuredDrafts.title: Association Between a Hybrid Video-Guided Multicomponent Exercise Program With Staff Assistance and Free-Living Gait in Older Adults With Knee and Low Back Pain: Secondary Analysis of a Randomized Controlled Trial
featuredDrafts.abstract: Older adults with chronic joint pain often exhibit decreased mobility. Daily walking measures are being increasingly used in aging research as  indicators of mobility.  In this study, we aimed to examine the effects of a 12-week hybrid exercise-based program on daily-life walking characteristics.  A total of 59 community-dwelling older adults (aged ≥65 years) with mild to moderate knee and/or low back pain were randomized to either a hybrid exercise group or an educational control group. Daily-life walking was monitored using an ankle sensor. Daily observation data were collected within 2 planned 7-day windows. Primary parameters included activity volume and gait characteristics. Statistical analyses were conducted based on a modified intention-to-treat principle using linear mixed-effects models, with a per-protocol set used for sensitivity analyses.  The mixed-effects analysis based on the modified intention-to-treat principle (n=52 participants; 696 observations) suggested an effect of the intervention on improving walking quality, particularly step length (β=2.39 cm; P =.04; Hedges g =0.493), with a smaller effect with borderline statistical significance observed on improving walking speed (β=0.05 m/s; P =.06; Hedges g =0.496). Cadence, daily distance, daily steps, active energy expenditure, and accumulated 3 or more metabolic equivalent of task activities showed no clear difference between the groups. In the per-protocol sensitivity analysis (n=44), the same directional pattern of improvement was observed for step length (β=1.95 cm; P =.13; Hedges g =0.365) and walking speed (β=0.04 m/s; P =.14; Hedges g =0.368); however, the estimates were imprecise.  A 12-week hybrid exercise program may improve the quality of daily-life walking, with the clearest effect observed on step length. Given the attenuation after multiplicity-aware interpretation and in sensitivity analyses, these findings should be interpreted as suggestive rather than definitive.

featuredDrafts.title: Deprescribing Fall Risk–Increasing Drugs in Older Adults: Implementation Challenges and a Conceptual Framework from the DeFRID Trial and Global Evidence
featuredDrafts.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
featuredDrafts.abstract: Deprescribing fall risk–increasing drugs (FRIDs) is essential for reducing polypharmacy and falls in older adults, yet randomized controlled trials (RCTs) face unique implementation challenges. The DeFRID study is an ongoing multi-center RCT evaluating an ARMOR-based deprescribing intervention versus usual care in adults aged ≥60 years prescribed FRIDs. The  of this review are threefold: (1) to describe practical challenges encountered during a multi-center deprescribing RCT in India; (2) to propose a conceptual framework for categorizing these barriers; and (3) to contextualize DeFRID's experience within the broader deprescribing research landscape.  We conducted a narrative review with systematic scoping elements, synthesizing global RCT evidence from PubMed, OpenAlex, and Google Scholar (inception–December 2025) with DeFRID process evaluation data. DeFRID barriers and facilitators were identified via mixed- (clinician KAP questionnaire and qualitative interviews), team meetings, retention logs, and Phase II RCT implementation data, thematically categorized, then compared with global RCT challenges.  DeFRID implementation revealed four challenge categories: ethical–clinical difficulties establishing equipoise for FRID withdrawal; operational barriers to recruitment and retention; methodological complexities in fall outcome ascertainment; and context-specific constraints unique to the Indian LMIC setting—limited deprescribing guidelines, polypharmacy normalization, fragmented care coordination, and hierarchical decision-making. Global RCTs revealed substantial implementation challenges: low clinician adherence, short follow-up periods, restrictive eligibility excluding frail or cognitively impaired older adults, and resource-intensive interventions limiting scalability.  Deprescribing FRIDs in older adults is impeded by ethical, operational, methodological, and provider-patient challenges, necessitating multilevel strategies integrating training, shared decision-making, context-specific guidelines, and stakeholder engagement for scalable implementation.

featuredDrafts.title: Sustaining agency after a fall: navigating healthcare and adjusting everyday life – a qualitative interview study
featuredDrafts.abstract: Falls among older adults are a major public health concern and are associated with recurrent falls, functional decline, fear of falling, and reduced quality of life. Older adults presenting to emergency departments (EDs) following a fall are often discharged directly home despite ongoing rehabilitation and support needs. Although person-centred approaches are recommended in international guidelines, less is known about older adults’ and relatives’ experiences following an ED visit for a fall. This study aimed to describe older adults’ and their relatives’ experiences of a fall, including the ED visit and the transition back home. Method A qualitative study design was used, involving semi-structured interviews with older adults aged 75 years and older and their relatives. Participants had attended the ED following a fall but were discharged without hospital admission. Seventeen participants (11 older adults and 6 relatives) were recruited. Data were analysed using qualitative content analysis according to Graneheim and Lundman.  The analysis generated one overarching theme, Sustaining agency through recovery across care and everyday life , which reflected how older adults and their relatives sought to manage daily life following a fall. Both groups described addressing immediate care needs while simultaneously adapting to longer-term changes in everyday life. Participants described difficulties navigating healthcare services to access follow-up care and rehabilitation, contributing to feelings of insecurity, financial strain, and increased responsibility. A persistent fear of falling affected daily activities and required adaptations and new roles for both older adults and their relatives. Despite these challenges, many participants demonstrated resilience and an ability to manage daily life following injury. Individual coping strategies and support from relatives were described as central to managing everyday life and healthcare contacts.  Older adults discharged home after a fall may benefit from coordinated, person-centred follow- up that supports rehabilitation, recovery, and fall prevention. Despite variation in support needs, participants described a common need for clearer guidance and improved support structures, while also demonstrating considerable resilience and capacity for self-management. featuredDrafts.title: Socioeconomic Differences in the Association Between the Big Five Personality Traits and Episodic Memory Trajectories in Midlife and Old Age
featuredDrafts.abstract: : Episodic memory trajectories vary substantially between individuals in the second half of life: some maintain high levels of performance into their 80s, whereas others experience marked declines as early as their 50s. Identifying factors that help explain this heterogeneity is critical for understanding cognitive aging. Drawing on the resource substitution hypothesis and the Openness–Fluid–Crystallized–Intelligence (OFCI) model, this preregistered study examined whether the Big Five personality traits and their interactions with socioeconomic status (SES) predict individual differences in episodic memory trajectories, testing also potential non-linear associations. We expected higher openness and lower neuroticism to be associated with better memory levels and slower decline, with stronger effects at lower levels of SES. : We analyzed data from 57,947 individuals aged 50 and older (M = 67.78, SD = 9.03) who participated in at least two waves (7, 8, or 9) of the Survey of Health, Ageing, and Retirement in Europe (SHARE). Multilevel growth models were used to estimate associations between personality and episodic memory levels and 5-year change, and whether SES (i.e., education, income, and wealth) moderated these associations. : Consistent with the OFCI model and the resource substitution hypothesis, higher openness was associated with better episodic memory levels, particularly among individuals with lower wealth. Higher neuroticism and lower conscientiousness were linked to poorer episodic memory levels, but only among less wealthy individuals. Higher extraversion was associated with better memory levels overall, and individuals at the extremes of extraversion exhibited somewhat flatter declines compared to those with moderate levels. Except for extraversion, there was little evidence for non-linear associations or for associations with 5-year change in episodic memory. : Our findings underscore the relevance of wealth as an important socioeconomic resource for cognitive health beyond income and education, particularly in old age, when income is typically reduced. Overall, the  support modest concurrent associations between personality, SES, and episodic memory levels, but provide hardly any evidence for longitudinal effects. More frequent and longer-term longitudinal assessments are needed to clarify potential effects on cognitive aging.

featuredDrafts.title: Large Language Model–Based Identification of Subjective Cognitive Decline in Electronic Health Records Among Older Adults With Normal Cognitive Testing: Retrospective Cohort Study
featuredDrafts.abstract: Subjective cognitive decline (SCD) typically refers to self- or informant-reported decline in cognition despite the absence of  impairment on standardized testing. Older adults with documented normal cognitive test performance provide a pragmatic anchor cohort for electronic health record (EHR)–based SCD phenotyping. However, cognitive concerns are primarily recorded in unstructured notes and are inconsistently documented, making it unclear how often and in whom concerns are captured in routine care.  This study aims to operationalize EHR-based SCD phenotyping in an objectively normal-testing cohort using a large language model (LLM)–based natural language processing approach and to examine the frequency and clinical and sociodemographic correlates of cognitive concern documentation.  We conducted an EHR-based observational study of patients aged 65 years or older with a first normal cognitive test recorded in EHR flowsheets between January 2019 and April 2024 in a large health care system. We developed and iteratively refined a 2-stage LLM-based natural language processing pipeline to identify documented cognitive concerns in unstructured notes during the 12 months prior to the index date, and evaluated performance against manual review. We quantified the frequency of documented concerns within this normal-testing cohort and used multivariable logistic regression to assess associations with sociodemographic factors (age, marital status, insurance, and neighborhood Area Deprivation Index), sequentially adjusting for clinical comorbidities and relevant medications.  Among 15,750 older adults with normal cognitive test scores, 13.8% (n=2175) had at least 1 documented cognitive concern in the prior year, captured in 1.2% (7394/605,177) of notes. On manual validation, the 2-stage pipeline (Med42-v2-8B screening followed by GPT-4o confirmation) achieved a sensitivity of 0.957, positive predictive value of 0.935, specificity of 0.985, and F 1 -score of 0.945 for cognitive concern identification. Documentation was more likely in older individuals, those with commercial (vs Medicare) insurance, and those with neurological and psychiatric conditions. In fully adjusted models, Parkinson disease (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 5.29, 95% CI 3.60‐7.77), traumatic brain injury (aOR 4.63, 95% CI 3.15‐6.81), stroke or transient ischemic attack (aOR 3.46, 95% CI 3.15‐4.18), epilepsy (aOR 2.52, 95% CI 1.83‐3.49), depression (aOR 1.54, 95% CI 1.36‐1.75), and excessive alcohol use (aOR 1.48, 95% CI 1.06‐2.06) were among the strongest correlates of cognitive concern documentation. In contrast, obesity (aOR 0.73, 95% CI 0.65‐0.82), hyperlipidemia (aOR 0.59, 95% CI 0.51‐0.67), and residence in more deprived neighborhoods (higher Area Deprivation Index) were associated with lower odds of documented cognitive concerns.  A 2-stage LLM pipeline enabled accurate identification of documented cognitive concerns consistent with SCD among older adults with normal cognitive testing. Documentation was uncommon and selectively captured by clinical and sociodemographic factors, with implications for equity and the validity of EHR-based phenotypes.
