featuredDrafts.title: Blind giving predicts longitudinal increases in scam susceptibility in later life
featuredDrafts.abstract: and  Financial fraud is a common and consequential threat among older adults, with estimated prevalence rates ranging from 4% to 17% annually. Although cognitive decline has been widely studied as a risk factor, less is known about behavioral characteristics that may predict changes in scam susceptibility. In the present study, we examined whether blind giving predicted trajectories of scam susceptibility across a two-year period and whether this association differed as a function of age. Research Design and  One hundred and sixteen cognitively unimpaired older adults (aged 51 to 83; 72% female) completed a behavioral economic measure of blind giving at baseline and a self-report measure of scam susceptibility annually across three visits.  Linear mixed-effects models revealed a significant interaction between time, blind giving, and age (p = .022), such that greater baseline blind giving was associated with increasing scam susceptibility over time among relatively older participants, whereas scam susceptibility remained stable across levels of blind giving among relatively younger participants. Blind giving was not associated with scam susceptibility at baseline (p = .515), and the longitudinal association persisted after separately adjusting for global cognition, socioeconomic status, and race (all ps ≤ .026).  Greater blind giving predicted longitudinal increases in scam susceptibility over a two-year period, with this pattern observed specifically in advanced age. These findings suggest that prosocial tendencies may become maladaptive in later life, underscoring the importance of identifying at-risk individuals to inform prevention efforts in aging populations.

featuredDrafts.title: Heat stress and coping strategies among older adults in three Sunbelt cities in the United States
featuredDrafts.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
featuredDrafts.abstract: Prevailing scientific evidence suggests that extreme heat poses a substantial threat to the health and well-being of older adults in the Sunbelt cities of the United States. However, prior research has not adequately addressed the specific socio-demographic, health-related vulnerabilities, and coping-strategic factors influencing heat stress among older urban populations.  Informed by the Socio-Ecological Model, this study adopts a retrospective cohort study design to investigate the predictors and experiences of heat stress among older adults. Data from older adults in Los Angeles, Houston, and Phoenix were analyzed using thematic and multiple binary logistic regression analyses.  The  reveal that much older adults (aged 80 +) were less likely to experience heat stress compared to their relatively younger counterparts. Also, marital status, income, respiratory diseases, physical activity, taking cool showers, and city of residence were significantly associated with a higher risk of suffering heat stress. The qualitative  uncovered individual-level behavioural adjustment as an effective coping mechanism during extreme heat events.  These  underscore the complex interplay of behavioral, socio-demographic, and health-related factors influencing heat stress among older adults. The study recommends that urban health strategies prioritize these demographics, enhancing support systems and coping mechanisms to reduce vulnerability to heat stress among older urban populations.

featuredDrafts.title: Being Sensed, Scored, and ‘Connected’: A Social-Gerontological Critique of AI-Driven Loneliness Detection for Older Adults in Taiwan
featuredDrafts.abstract: Enthusiasm for artificial intelligence (AI) that continuously infers emotion promises to change how care systems identify older adults at risk of loneliness. We use AI-driven loneliness detection to mean systems that infer loneliness, or a proxy for it, from sensed data rather than from a person’s answer, rendering the inference as a score or category used in care; they range from facial and vocal emotion recognition to behavioral risk prediction from everyday activity data. Engineering feasibility, more than any social-gerontological understanding of loneliness, has driven this agenda, and little attention has gone to how older adults in different cultural contexts wish to be known and supported. Because such detection is not yet in routine use in Taiwan, this Forum article adopts an anticipatory-governance stance, examining before deployment a trajectory that policy makes plausible. Anchored in Taiwan’s ageing society and long-term care system, it argues that culturally responsive design should begin with older adults’ own meanings, relational obligations, and expectations of privacy and autonomy, not with the sensors. It identifies three tensions for social gerontology: the reframing of a relational experience as an individual biometric deficit; the risk that algorithms read culturally patterned emotional restraint as noise; and the slippage from care toward surveillance once risk indices enter routine care workflows. Taking seriously the case for technological augmentation of scarce care resources, the article proposes principles for a socially accountable approach and a research agenda on how older adults negotiate being sensed, scored, and ‘connected.’

featuredDrafts.title: Vulnerability Intersections: An Integrative Conceptual Framework for Understanding Vulnerability in AI-Assisted Care for Older Adults
featuredDrafts.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) applications are increasingly used to support independent living and care for older adults, particularly those in vulnerable situations. Yet, how vulnerability is constructed when AI enters later-life care remains poorly theorized. Existing approaches to vulnerability in old age inadequately address AI-related risks, structural conditions, exposure pathways, and life course disadvantages. Using a theory-synthesis approach, this article proposes “vulnerability intersections” as an integrative framework for how vulnerability is constructed, enacted, and negotiated in AI-assisted care for older adults. The framework extends existing sociotechnical accounts by conceptualizing vulnerability as taking four overlapping forms: anticipatory, opaque, routinized, and normative. It locates vulnerability factors at the micro level of older adults’ lives, the meso level of care organizations and technology providers, and the macro level of political-economic and regulatory arrangements, with life-course accumulation spanning all three. It also proposes three exposure pathways through which vulnerability factors become consequential: AI-mediated information and representations of aging; AI-powered care organization and delivery; and AI-configured power, participation, and social relations. The framework shifts attention away from viewing older adults as inherently vulnerable toward examining the sociotechnical arrangements under which vulnerability is anticipated, classified, distributed, and negotiated when AI enters care.

featuredDrafts.title: Mental health literacy and help-seeking behaviour among older adults in Mysuru, India: a mixed methods study
featuredDrafts.abstract: As populations age globally, mental health remains a frequently neglected aspect of healthy ageing. Older adults face biological, psychological, and social challenges that heighten their risk of mental health problems, yet professional service utilization remains low. In India, this treatment gap is worsened by limited mental health literacy, stigma, and socio-cultural barriers. This study assessed mental health literacy and help-seeking behaviour among older adults in Mysuru, examined their association, and explored barriers and facilitators influencing professional help-seeking.  An explanatory sequential mixed- design was used. A community-based cross-sectional survey was conducted among 232 older adults (aged ≥ 60 years) selected through multistage stratified sampling from rural and urban Mysuru Taluk, Karnataka. Mental health literacy was measured using the Mental Health Literacy Scale (MHLS) and help-seeking behaviour using the Attitudes Toward Seeking Professional Psychological Help Scale (ATSPPH). Non-parametric tests and Spearman’s correlation were applied. Eight in-depth interviews followed, analyzed using Braun and Clarke’s thematic analysis and Lewin’s Force Field Analysis framework.  Participants had a median MHLS score of 105 (IQR 12), representing a substantial proportion of the maximum possible score of 160, yet only 7.8% had sought professional help in the preceding 12 months, with most turning first to family or friends. A significant negative correlation existed between mental health literacy and help-seeking attitudes (ρ = -0.262, p  Despite a comparatively favourable median mental health literacy score, professional help-seeking among older adults in Mysuru remains limited. featuredDrafts.title: Functional status and depressive symptoms in relation to bone mineral density and osteoporosis in hospitalized older adults: a cross-sectional study
featuredDrafts.abstract: Introduction Osteoporosis is a major cause of morbidity and fractures among older adults, contributing substantially to disability, hospitalization, and mortality. This cross-sectional study investigated the associations of depressive symptoms and functional status with bone mineral density (BMD) and osteoporosis in hospitalized older adults.  We analyzed 1,048 hospitalized patients aged ≥ 70 years who underwent dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA). Depressive symptoms (GDS-15) and functional status (Barthel Index) were extracted from routine geriatric assessments. Group comparisons, multivariable linear regression, and logistic regression analyses were performed after adjustment for demographic, clinical, and endocrine covariates.  Lower Barthel Index scores and higher depressive symptom burden were independently associated with lower hip BMD, whereas associations with lumbar spine BMD were less consistent. Although statistically significant, the observed effect sizes were modest. The multivariable model explained a moderate proportion of BMD variability (adjusted R² = 0.22).  Functional and psychological characteristics were independently associated with bone mineral density in hospitalized older adults. Given the cross-sectional design, causal relationships cannot be established. These findings support the potential value of incorporating comprehensive geriatric assessment into osteoporosis evaluation to improve identification of older adults at increased fracture risk.

featuredDrafts.title: Components of family empowerment for family caregivers of older adults with dementia: focus group interviews
featuredDrafts.abstract: Strengthening empowerment plays a pivotal role in supporting family caregivers of older adults with dementia. This study explored the comprehensive caregiving experiences of both family caregivers and dementia care professionals to identify and describe the components of family empowerment within the Korean context.  A qualitative study was conducted using semi-structured focus group interviews (FGIs). Participants included 14 family caregivers (3 groups) and 5 Dementia care professionals (1 group). Psychological Empowerment Model (PEM) served as the theoretical framework to understand the dimensions of empowerment. The specific components of empowerment in Korean family caregivers of older adults with dementia were analyzed using qualitative thematic analysis.  Seven main themes and 14 sub-themes were identified as components of family empowerment. The main themes included: (1) Reconstructing the caregiving situation and awareness; (2) Acquiring dementia information through experiential means; (3) Satisfaction with doing my best in caregiving; (4) Balance between self-care and family care; (5) Securing and utilizing dementia-related resources; (6) Reflections of caregiving experiences; and (7) New roles and relationships created through caregiving.  The findings of the study elucidate that family empowerment of family caregivers of older adults with dementia is a multidimensional construct: it is established through the cognitive process of reconstructing caregiving perceptions, emotional fulfillment derived from the stability of the caregiving process, behavioral practices of balancing self-care with family care, and relational reinforcement gained through newly established roles. Future efforts should establish sustainable support systems through education, resource linkage, and emotional support. Additionally, we propose the development of empowerment intervention programs and measurement tools based on these identified components. Clinical trial number Not applicable.

featuredDrafts.title: Associations of Midlife Gait Speed and Muscle Performance With Falls in Later Life: Secondary Analysis of the MIDUS Cohort
featuredDrafts.abstract: Falls are a major cause of morbidity among older adults, yet fall risk may begin to emerge during midlife. Physical performance measures may identify early functional vulnerability associated with later-life health outcomes.  This study examined whether midlife gait speed and muscle performance were associated with recurrent falls later in life.  This study was a secondary analysis of prospectively collected data from the Midlife in the United States (MIDUS) cohort. Independent adults (n=309) aged 45 to 64 years at wave 2 (2004-2009) who completed physical performance assessments were followed to wave 3 (2013-2021). Baseline measures included gait speed from a 50-foot walk test, grip strength, sit-to-stand time, and calculated lower-extremity power. The primary analysis examined associations between baseline physical performance and recurrent falls at follow-up (≥2 falls in the previous 12 months). A sensitivity analysis repeated the primary models but was restricted to participants without a baseline history of recurrent falls.  At follow-up, 20.4% (63/309) of participants reported recurrent falls. Slower midlife gait speed was associated with higher odds of recurrent falls (odds ratio 1.43, 95% CI 1.05-1.95; P=.02), whereas muscle performance measures were not associated with falls in the primary analysis. The association between slower gait speed and recurrent falls remained significant in the sensitivity analysis. Over follow-up, muscle performance declined, whereas gait speed remained stable.  Slower midlife gait speed was associated with higher odds of recurrent falls, suggesting that fall vulnerability may be detectable as early as midlife. Given the exploratory nature of this study, further studies are warranted to confirm these findings.

featuredDrafts.title: Planetary Health Diet Adherence and Frailty in Older Adults: Evidence from the Seniors-ENRICA Cohorts
featuredDrafts.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
featuredDrafts.abstract: Frailty is a major determinant of disability and adverse outcomes in older adults. The Planetary Health Diet (PHD), a plant-based dietary pattern promoting environmental sustainability, has been associated with lower mortality and reduced chronic disease risk. We examined the association between adherence to the Planetary Health Diet Index (PHDI) and frailty over time using repeated frailty assessments.  Data came from two cohorts of community-dwelling older adults: Seniors-ENRICA-1 (2008-2015; ≥60 years; n = 3,289) and Seniors-ENRICA-2 (2015-2023; ≥65 years; n = 3,273). Baseline diet was assessed using a validated diet history, and adherence to the PHD was assessed using the PHDI (0-140), based on 15 food groups. Frailty was defined by the Fried phenotype (≥3 criteria of exhaustion, low physical activity, slow gait, muscle weakness, unintentional weight loss). Generalized estimating equation (GEE) models estimated odds ratios (OR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) for frailty across PHDI tertiles, adjusting for sociodemographic, lifestyle, and clinical factors.  Higher PHDI adherence was consistently associated with lower odds of frailty over time. Comparing highest vs. lowest tertiles, multivariable-adjusted ORs (95% CI) were 0.62 (0.42, 0.92) in Seniors-ENRICA-1, 0.40 (0.24, 0.65) in Seniors-ENRICA-2 and 0.52 (0.38, 0.70) in the pooled analyses. Higher PHDI adherence was primarily associated with lower odds of low physical activity, while vegetables and fruits showed the strongest independent associations among individual PHDI components.  Greater PHDI adherence is associated with lower odds of frailty in Spanish older adults, supporting the potential role of sustainable, plant-based dietary patterns for healthy ageing.

archiveRecords.title: Location, Location, Location: How Community Distress Shapes Physical and Mental Health Outcomes for Caregiving Grandparents
archiveRecords.abstract: The health of caregiving grandparents is a critical area of research. Financial strain is a well-established predictor of health and a common issue for caregiving grandparents.  We sought to understand how community context influences this relationship between financial strain and health. Specifically, we examined two dimensions of community context: community distress and perceived access to key resources for caregiving.  Using a sample of caregiving grandparents ( N = 439), we first conducted Latent Class Analysis to identify distinct profiles of resource access. We then used moderated mediation analyses to test whether financial well-being mediated the relationship between community distress and health, and whether this indirect effect varied by resource access profile.  We found the relation between community distress and health through financial well-being varies depending on the grandparents’ perceived resource access. This research points to the importance of community context in the lives of grandparent caregivers.

archiveRecords.title: Admission lactate-to-albumin ratio in critically ill older adults: superior to its individual components but not additive to APACHE II — a retrospective cohort study
archiveRecords.abstract: Older adults constitute a growing and heterogeneous proportion of intensive care unit (ICU) admissions, and early risk stratification in this group remains difficult. The lactate-to-albumin ratio (LAR) is a composite biomarker that combines a marker of acute metabolic derangement with one of physiological reserve, and has shown prognostic value in several critical care settings. Its performance in geriatric ICU patients, and specifically whether it adds information to established severity scores, has not been established.  We conducted a retrospective, single-centre cohort study of consecutive patients aged ≥ 65 years admitted to the mixed medical–surgical ICU of a tertiary referral hospital in Türkiye between January 2024 and July 2025. LAR was calculated as serum lactate (mmol/L) divided by serum albumin (g/dL), from samples obtained within the first 6 h of ICU admission. The primary outcome was all-cause 28-day mortality. Discrimination was assessed by area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), and curves were compared using the DeLong test. Multivariable logistic regression assessed whether LAR was independently associated with mortality after adjustment for age, sex, Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS), SOFA, APACHE II and C-reactive protein (CRP).  Of 296 screened admissions, 294 were analysed; 98 patients (33.3%) died within 28 days. Non-survivors had higher admission LAR than survivors [1.37 (IQR 0.84–2.50) vs. 0.62 (IQR 0.46–0.99), p p = 0.0005) and serum albumin alone (AUC 0.656; ΔAUC 0.137, 95% CI 0.061–0.213, p = 0.0004). APACHE II discriminated considerably better than LAR (AUC 0.924, 95% CI 0.893–0.955; ΔAUC 0.131, 95% CI 0.080–0.181, p p = 0.055; likelihood ratio test p = 0.098). On univariable analysis LAR was strongly associated with mortality (OR 2.17, 95% CI 1.63–2.88, p p = 0.052). APACHE II (adjusted OR 1.36, 95% CI 1.21–1.52, p p = 0.015) remained independently associated with mortality.  In critically ill older adults, admission LAR discriminates 28-day mortality better than either of its components alone and is strongly associated with mortality on unadjusted analysis. However, it did not add significant discriminatory information to the APACHE II score, and it was not independently associated with mortality after adjustment for illness severity. LAR may be useful as a rapidly available early indicator where a full severity score is not yet computable, but on these data it does not complement APACHE II.

archiveRecords.title: Ageism and Quality of Life in Older Adults: The Roles of Self-Disgust and Psychological Distress
archiveRecords.abstract: This study examined psychological correlates of quality of life (QoL) among older adults in a Latin American context, focussing on the roles of ageism, self-disgust, and psychological distress. Hierarchical multiple regression analyses were used to examine the incremental contribution of sociodemographic factors, three dimensions of ageism, self-disgust, and psychological distress to QoL among 272 Colombian older adults (mean age = 68.40, SD = 6.80). Findings indicated that interpersonal experiences of ageism, but not exposure to ageist messages or self-ageism, were associated with poorer QoL. Higher self-disgust and psychological distress were independently associated with lower QoL and formed part of a significant indirect association between interpersonal ageism and QoL. These findings suggest that quality of life in later adulthood is associated not only with structural and sociodemographic conditions, but also with psychological processes through which age-related stigma may be experienced and internalised. Interventions that reduce interpersonal ageism while promoting self-acceptance and more positive views of ageing may represent promising avenues for supporting wellbeing and quality of life in older adults.

archiveRecords.title: Age Effects in Story Recall: Comparing the Narrative Similarities of Memories for a Fictional Movie
archiveRecords.journal: The International Journal of Aging and Human Development
archiveRecords.abstract: This study examines age differences in memories for a fictional story. We compared the narratives of young and older participants about a TV series when recalled to a young or older listener. In the young listener condition, 35 older and 37 young adults recalled the episode to a young adult. In the older listener condition, 40 older and 37 young participants recalled it to an older adult. Memories were analyzed with three complementary : (1) a measure of episodic specificity, (2) a quantification of semantic similarity, and (3) the lexical content.  revealed that young adults had more similar memories than older adults, and used more words related to negative emotions than older adults. archiveRecords.title: Intrinsic Capacity in a Nationally Representative US Population
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: Intrinsic capacity (IC) is defined by the World Health Organization as the sum of an individual’s physical and mental abilities that support health and well-being. While well validated internationally, it has not been operationalized and validated in a nationally representative US cohort.  Using data from 5,834 community-dwelling older adults from Round 12 (2022) of the National Health and Aging Trends Study (NHATS) survey, we identified measures related to IC domains (cognition, locomotion, vitality, psychological, sensory). We performed exploratory factor analysis (EFA), omega hierarchical reliability testing, and confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) using bi-factor and second-order structures. We also constructed the Integrated Care for Older People (ICOPE) screening tool. Descriptive statistics and regression models were used to examine the associations of IC and ICOPE scores with demographic and health characteristics. Age- and sex-specific reference centile curves were developed using empirical percentiles.  EFA consistently supported a six-factor structure (vision and hearing were separate). Omega hierarchical analysis supported a strong general factor (ω = 0.92; ωₕ=0.72), and the bi-factor model demonstrated excellent fit. IC and ICOPE scores showed strong correlation (r = 0.71). Higher IC scores were associated with younger age, higher level of education, and income. Prevalence of comorbidities, frailty, ADL and IADL disability increased from the highest to the lowest IC and ICOPE quartiles. Reference centile curves demonstrated progressive age-related decline, with females showing lower IC scores than males.  We demonstrate IC operationalization in a nationally representative U.S. cohort and provide the first US-specific reference centile curves. The findings provide a foundation for future IC research in the US.

archiveRecords.title: Exploring Heterogeneity in Smartphone Addiction Risk Among Community-Dwelling Older Adults in Guangzhou: A Machine Learning Analysis
archiveRecords.abstract: Smartphone addiction risk is an underexamined concern in later life, and prior research often treats older adults as a homogeneous group. Using cross-sectional survey data from 2,275 community-dwelling adults aged 60 years or older in Guangzhou, this exploratory study applied XGBoost with SHAP analysis to identify predictive correlates, followed by K-means clustering to examine subgroup heterogeneity among participants classified as high risk. Social participation and depressive symptoms were associated with the risk with nonlinear patterns. Two exploratory profiles were identified: the Socially Active profile (40.7%), characterized by high participation and more regular non-kin contacts, and the Emotionally Withdrawn profile (59.3%), characterized by elevated depressive symptoms, fewer regular non-kin contacts, and entertainment-oriented use. The findings lend credence to the paradigms of social overload and emotional compensation and suggest that digital inclusion among older adults must be coupled with support for digital self-regulation, psychological well-being, and social and family engagements.

archiveRecords.title: Nurse-administered symptom-burden screening and 12-month mortality in older adults with heart failure: a cohort study
archiveRecords.abstract: Older adults with heart failure face significant symptoms and psychosocial burdens that routine cardiology care might overlook. We assessed whether Edmonton Symptom Assessment System (ESAS) and Integrated Palliative Care Outcome Scale (IPOS) scores can predict 12-month mortality and improve risk discrimination beyond clinical covariates in a hospital cohort from a low-resource setting.  We conducted an observational cohort study at the National Geriatric Hospital (Vietnam). Inpatients aged 60 years or older with chronic heart failure who met the eligibility criteria were approached in the order of admission (January 2021-December 2022), and ESAS (9 items, each scored 0–10) and IPOS (17 items) were completed within 48 h of admission by trained ward nurse-researchers. Vital status at 12 months was determined through medical records and structured follow-up calls. Cox proportional hazards models evaluated associations with mortality, adjusting for age, sex, heart-failure classification, New York Heart Association (NYHA) class, comorbidities, and financial strain. Primary analyses used predefined categorical cutoffs (ESAS > 30; IPOS ≥ 20). Discrimination was further assessed with Harrell’s C-index and the 12-month area under the curve (AUC), and model fit was compared using Akaike and Bayesian information criteria. Calibration was also examined using a logistic analogue (Hosmer–Lemeshow).  Of 327 screened patients, 304 were enrolled (mean age 71.9 ± 8.8 years; 52% men); 65 deaths (21.4%) occurred within 12 months. ESAS and IPOS were strongly correlated, but there was no multicollinearity. High symptom burden (ESAS > 30) independently predicted mortality (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR] 2.27; 95%CI 1.20–4.28), while high palliative-care needs (IPOS ≥ 20) were not associated (aHR: 1.04; 95%CI 0.47–2.30). Kaplan–Meier curves across ESAS–IPOS strata diverged. Including categorical patient-reported measures in the clinical model modestly improved discrimination and fit: Harrell’s C increased from 0.671 to 0.697 and 12-month AUC from 0.700 to 0.718 ( p = 0.034), with acceptable calibration and lower information criteria.  In hospitalized older adults with heart failure, a nurse-administered ESAS identified patients at independently higher 12-month mortality risk. IPOS, though clinically informative for care planning, added little prognostic information once symptom severity was considered. Brief, nurse-led symptom screening offers a feasible approach to risk stratification in resource-limited settings. Trial registration Not applicable.

archiveRecords.title: Characterizing lesbian, gay, and bisexual patients’ experiences with elder abuse: A chart review study
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: Older adults who identify as lesbian, gay, or bisexual (LGB) may be at increased risk of elder abuse (EA) due to unique risk factors; however, research in healthcare settings has been limited by the lack of data on sexual orientation. Since 2022, the Veterans Health Administration (VHA) has collected self-reported sexual orientation for all patients. The  of this chart review study was to use newly available electronic health record (EHR) data to explore the documented experiences of older LGB adults identified with EA concerns.  We randomly sampled 100 of 201 Veterans aged ≥60 years with an outpatient visit between 10/2022-9/2023 who identified as LGB and had a social work visit for possible abuse/neglect. We conducted protocolized chart reviews of clinical notes within ±180 days of the social work visit for 23 LGB patients, with EHR documentation confirming EA, to describe key characteristics and documented EA experiences.  Among 23 EA cases in LGB Veterans, 8 (35%) had cognitive impairment, 8 (35%) reported a history of child maltreatment, and 7 (30%) reported military sexual trauma. Veterans’ sexual orientation was sometimes noted to contribute to past abuse experiences; however, the relationship between sexual orientation and EA or EA care processes was rarely documented by clinicians. Discussion Findings highlight important considerations for sexual orientation minority patients experiencing EA, including opportunities to examine both contributors to EA risk among older LGB patients and to address LGB-specific care needs for this population in future research.

archiveRecords.title: Multimorbidity, Polypharmacy, and Neighborhood Disadvantage as Determinants of Cognitive Performance in the ARCHES Cohort
archiveRecords.abstract: African American adults experience a disproportionate burden of dementia, shaped by structural and clinical factors that remain unclear.  To quantify associations between multimorbidity, polypharmacy, and cognition in the context of neighborhood disadvantage.  This study is a cross-sectional analysis of 348 African American adults aged 45–92 years (mean 64.3 years; 73.6% female) from the Aging Research Characterizing Health Exposome via Social drivers (ARCHES) cohort. Comorbidity burden was assessed using a modified Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI), polypharmacy as ≥5 medications, and neighborhood disadvantage using the Area Deprivation Index (ADI). Linear regression estimated associations with a Preclinical Alzheimer’s Cognitive Composite (PACC). The polypharmacy model included modified CCI as a covariate, and effect modification by ADI was assessed using an interaction term between polypharmacy and ADI.  Higher modified CCI was associated with lower cognitive performance (B = −0.071; 95% CI: −0.130, −0.012). Polypharmacy was not independently associated with cognition after modified CCI adjustment (B = −0.081; β = −0.057; p = 0.257). No significant ADI interaction was found (p = 0.064).

archiveRecords.title: Chronic inflammation and multiple dimensions of aging among women in the Philippines
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: Age-related increases in chronic systemic inflammation are strong predictors of morbidity and mortality in high income countries, but evidence is lacking from lower- and middle-income settings where infectious diseases are more prevalent and rates of overweight and obesity are relatively low. Here we evaluate two complementary measures of chronic inflammation—plasma C-reactive protein (CRP) and a DNA methylation–based surrogate (DNAm-CRP)—measured at baseline as predictors of physical capacity, cognitive function, and cardiometabolic disease seven years later among women in the Philippines (N = 953; 43-75 years at follow-up). Levels of CRP and DNAm-CRP were not strongly associated with age. Both measures predicted subsequent declines in physical and functional capacity, increased incidence of diabetes and hypertension, and poorer cognitive performance, after adjustment for baseline status and other covariates. DNAm-CRP performed comparably to CRP, and was robust to variation in white blood cell composition and acute infectious symptoms at the time of sampling. These findings demonstrate that chronic inflammation is associated with multiple dimensions of aging in a lower-middle income setting, and highlights the utility of inflammatory biomarkers as scalable tools for global aging research.

archiveRecords.title: Societal actors’ perceptions of intersectoral collaboration and the participation of older adults in the development of age-friendly environments
archiveRecords.abstract: Older adults’ participation and intersectoral collaboration are central to the development of age-friendly environments. While previous research has emphasised the importance of these principles, less is known about how they are understood and enacted by societal actors in practice. This creates a need to explore societal actors’ perceptions of both intersectoral collaboration and older adults’ participation in the development of age-friendly environments. Method The study had a participatory qualitative design. Data were collected through a World Café involving 19 societal actors in a Swedish municipal context. Participants represented several societal sectors relevant to age-friendly environments, including welfare, care, public health, governance, social sustainability, urban planning,mobility, civil society, and voluntary engagement. Findings The findings showed that participants perceived intersectoral collaboration as requiring shared societal responsibility across multiple sectors, while responsibility risked becoming unclear when no actor had an explicit mandate to coordinate, prioritise and act. Intersectoral collaboration was viewed as a way of sharing resources, yet also as vulnerable when it relied mainly on personal relationships and informal networks rather than organisationally embedded structures. Similarly, older adults’ participation was highly valued when developing age-friendly initiatives, but participants questioned whether existing participation channels adequately reflect the diversity of older adults’ experiences and needs.  Age-friendly work requires shared responsibility across societal actors, supported by clear coordination. Personal relationships and informal networks should be recognised as valuable for enabling collaboration, but they need to be complemented by formal structures to ensure sustainability over time. Moreover, greater efforts to reach seldom-heard older adults are needed. Doing so may contribute to more nuanced and age-friendly initiatives that better reflect the diverse needs of the older population.

archiveRecords.title: Safe homecoming intervention after hospital discharge: a retrospective cohort study of mortality and readmission among patients 75 years or older in Sweden
archiveRecords.abstract: After a hospital stay, older patients are at increased risk of health complications that may lead to readmission to hospital or premature death. Globally, numerous interventions have been applied to enhance transitional care for older patients, but the evidence base remains inconclusive. One form of a transitional care intervention is the Swedish primary health care Safe homecoming intervention, a time-limited, interprofessional and tailored home health care intervention designed to prevent avoidable complications and readmissions following hospital discharge. The effects of Safe homecoming have not yet been scientifically evaluated. The present study aimed to assess the association between the interprofessional Safe h omecoming intervention and the risk of death or readmission.  We conducted a retrospective propensity score-matched cohort study in Örebro County, Sweden, using administrative and medical-record data from 2013 to 2020. The source cohort comprised 38,338 patients aged 75 years or older who had been admitted to hospital for at least one day. We included 128 patients who received the interprofessional Safe homecoming intervention at a single primary health care centre between 1 November 2016 and 31 May 2019 and 512 propensity score-matched controls from across the county receiving standard care.  The mean age was 85.5 years, and 60.9% of patients in both groups were women. At 90 days, the cumulative incidence of first hospital readmission was 20.3% in the intervention group and 33.6% among controls (Gray’s test p = 0.005). In the competing-risk analysis, the Fine-Gray subdistribution hazard ratio was 0.57 (95% CI 0.37–0.86; p = 0.008). The corresponding cause-specific Cox model yielded an HR of 0.55 (95% CI 0.36–0.84; p = 0.005). At 365 days, the Fine-Gray estimate was 0.79 (95% CI 0.59–1.05; p = 0.098). Mortality estimates favoured the intervention group numerically but were imprecise, with confidence intervals including the null at all evaluated follow-up times.  The Safe Homecoming intervention was associated with a lower risk of first hospital readmission at 90 days, whereas there was no clear evidence of an association with mortality or longer-term readmission. Given the observational design, small intervention sample, potential residual confounding and evaluation of multiple follow-up time points, these findings should be considered exploratory and require confirmation in larger prospective studies.

reviewRecords.title: Location, Location, Location: How Community Distress Shapes Physical and Mental Health Outcomes for Caregiving Grandparents
reviewRecords.abstract: The health of caregiving grandparents is a critical area of research. Financial strain is a well-established predictor of health and a common issue for caregiving grandparents.  We sought to understand how community context influences this relationship between financial strain and health. Specifically, we examined two dimensions of community context: community distress and perceived access to key resources for caregiving.  Using a sample of caregiving grandparents ( N = 439), we first conducted Latent Class Analysis to identify distinct profiles of resource access. We then used moderated mediation analyses to test whether financial well-being mediated the relationship between community distress and health, and whether this indirect effect varied by resource access profile.  We found the relation between community distress and health through financial well-being varies depending on the grandparents’ perceived resource access. This research points to the importance of community context in the lives of grandparent caregivers.

reviewRecords.title: Ageism and Quality of Life in Older Adults: The Roles of Self-Disgust and Psychological Distress
reviewRecords.abstract: This study examined psychological correlates of quality of life (QoL) among older adults in a Latin American context, focussing on the roles of ageism, self-disgust, and psychological distress. Hierarchical multiple regression analyses were used to examine the incremental contribution of sociodemographic factors, three dimensions of ageism, self-disgust, and psychological distress to QoL among 272 Colombian older adults (mean age = 68.40, SD = 6.80). Findings indicated that interpersonal experiences of ageism, but not exposure to ageist messages or self-ageism, were associated with poorer QoL. Higher self-disgust and psychological distress were independently associated with lower QoL and formed part of a significant indirect association between interpersonal ageism and QoL. These findings suggest that quality of life in later adulthood is associated not only with structural and sociodemographic conditions, but also with psychological processes through which age-related stigma may be experienced and internalised. Interventions that reduce interpersonal ageism while promoting self-acceptance and more positive views of ageing may represent promising avenues for supporting wellbeing and quality of life in older adults.

reviewRecords.title: Age Effects in Story Recall: Comparing the Narrative Similarities of Memories for a Fictional Movie
reviewRecords.journal: The International Journal of Aging and Human Development
reviewRecords.abstract: This study examines age differences in memories for a fictional story. We compared the narratives of young and older participants about a TV series when recalled to a young or older listener. In the young listener condition, 35 older and 37 young adults recalled the episode to a young adult. In the older listener condition, 40 older and 37 young participants recalled it to an older adult. Memories were analyzed with three complementary : (1) a measure of episodic specificity, (2) a quantification of semantic similarity, and (3) the lexical content.  revealed that young adults had more similar memories than older adults, and used more words related to negative emotions than older adults. However, older adults recalled as many episodic details as younger participants. There was no difference as a function of the recipient's age. Overall, these  underscore the value of studying memory in everyday social contexts.

reviewRecords.title: Exploring Heterogeneity in Smartphone Addiction Risk Among Community-Dwelling Older Adults in Guangzhou: A Machine Learning Analysis
reviewRecords.abstract: Smartphone addiction risk is an underexamined concern in later life, and prior research often treats older adults as a homogeneous group. Using cross-sectional survey data from 2,275 community-dwelling adults aged 60 years or older in Guangzhou, this exploratory study applied XGBoost with SHAP analysis to identify predictive correlates, followed by K-means clustering to examine subgroup heterogeneity among participants classified as high risk. Social participation and depressive symptoms were associated with the risk with nonlinear patterns. Two exploratory profiles were identified: the Socially Active profile (40.7%), characterized by high participation and more regular non-kin contacts, and the Emotionally Withdrawn profile (59.3%), characterized by elevated depressive symptoms, fewer regular non-kin contacts, and entertainment-oriented use. The findings lend credence to the paradigms of social overload and emotional compensation and suggest that digital inclusion among older adults must be coupled with support for digital self-regulation, psychological well-being, and social and family engagements.

reviewRecords.title: Nurse-administered symptom-burden screening and 12-month mortality in older adults with heart failure: a cohort study
reviewRecords.abstract: Older adults with heart failure face significant symptoms and psychosocial burdens that routine cardiology care might overlook. We assessed whether Edmonton Symptom Assessment System (ESAS) and Integrated Palliative Care Outcome Scale (IPOS) scores can predict 12-month mortality and improve risk discrimination beyond clinical covariates in a hospital cohort from a low-resource setting.  We conducted an observational cohort study at the National Geriatric Hospital (Vietnam). Inpatients aged 60 years or older with chronic heart failure who met the eligibility criteria were approached in the order of admission (January 2021-December 2022), and ESAS (9 items, each scored 0–10) and IPOS (17 items) were completed within 48 h of admission by trained ward nurse-researchers. Vital status at 12 months was determined through medical records and structured follow-up calls. Cox proportional hazards models evaluated associations with mortality, adjusting for age, sex, heart-failure classification, New York Heart Association (NYHA) class, comorbidities, and financial strain. Primary analyses used predefined categorical cutoffs (ESAS > 30; IPOS ≥ 20). Discrimination was further assessed with Harrell’s C-index and the 12-month area under the curve (AUC), and model fit was compared using Akaike and Bayesian information criteria. Calibration was also examined using a logistic analogue (Hosmer–Lemeshow).  Of 327 screened patients, 304 were enrolled (mean age 71.9 ± 8.8 years; 52% men); 65 deaths (21.4%) occurred within 12 months. ESAS and IPOS were strongly correlated, but there was no multicollinearity. High symptom burden (ESAS > 30) independently predicted mortality (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR] 2.27; 95%CI 1.20–4.28), while high palliative-care needs (IPOS ≥ 20) were not associated (aHR: 1.04; 95%CI 0.47–2.30). Kaplan–Meier curves across ESAS–IPOS strata diverged. Including categorical patient-reported measures in the clinical model modestly improved discrimination and fit: Harrell’s C increased from 0.671 to 0.697 and 12-month AUC from 0.700 to 0.718 ( p = 0.034), with acceptable calibration and lower information criteria.  In hospitalized older adults with heart failure, a nurse-administered ESAS identified patients at independently higher 12-month mortality risk. IPOS, though clinically informative for care planning, added little prognostic information once symptom severity was considered. Brief, nurse-led symptom screening offers a feasible approach to risk stratification in resource-limited settings. Trial registration Not applicable.

reviewRecords.title: Characterizing lesbian, gay, and bisexual patients’ experiences with elder abuse: A chart review study
reviewRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
reviewRecords.abstract: Older adults who identify as lesbian, gay, or bisexual (LGB) may be at increased risk of elder abuse (EA) due to unique risk factors; however, research in healthcare settings has been limited by the lack of data on sexual orientation. Since 2022, the Veterans Health Administration (VHA) has collected self-reported sexual orientation for all patients. The  of this chart review study was to use newly available electronic health record (EHR) data to explore the documented experiences of older LGB adults identified with EA concerns.  We randomly sampled 100 of 201 Veterans aged ≥60 years with an outpatient visit between 10/2022-9/2023 who identified as LGB and had a social work visit for possible abuse/neglect. We conducted protocolized chart reviews of clinical notes within ±180 days of the social work visit for 23 LGB patients, with EHR documentation confirming EA, to describe key characteristics and documented EA experiences.  Among 23 EA cases in LGB Veterans, 8 (35%) had cognitive impairment, 8 (35%) reported a history of child maltreatment, and 7 (30%) reported military sexual trauma. Veterans’ sexual orientation was sometimes noted to contribute to past abuse experiences; however, the relationship between sexual orientation and EA or EA care processes was rarely documented by clinicians. Discussion Findings highlight important considerations for sexual orientation minority patients experiencing EA, including opportunities to examine both contributors to EA risk among older LGB patients and to address LGB-specific care needs for this population in future research.

reviewRecords.title: Multimorbidity, Polypharmacy, and Neighborhood Disadvantage as Determinants of Cognitive Performance in the ARCHES Cohort
reviewRecords.abstract: African American adults experience a disproportionate burden of dementia, shaped by structural and clinical factors that remain unclear.  To quantify associations between multimorbidity, polypharmacy, and cognition in the context of neighborhood disadvantage.  This study is a cross-sectional analysis of 348 African American adults aged 45–92 years (mean 64.3 years; 73.6% female) from the Aging Research Characterizing Health Exposome via Social drivers (ARCHES) cohort. Comorbidity burden was assessed using a modified Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI), polypharmacy as ≥5 medications, and neighborhood disadvantage using the Area Deprivation Index (ADI). Linear regression estimated associations with a Preclinical Alzheimer’s Cognitive Composite (PACC). The polypharmacy model included modified CCI as a covariate, and effect modification by ADI was assessed using an interaction term between polypharmacy and ADI.  Higher modified CCI was associated with lower cognitive performance (B = −0.071; 95% CI: −0.130, −0.012). Polypharmacy was not independently associated with cognition after modified CCI adjustment (B = −0.081; β = −0.057; p = 0.257). No significant ADI interaction was found (p = 0.064).

reviewRecords.title: Chronic inflammation and multiple dimensions of aging among women in the Philippines
reviewRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
reviewRecords.abstract: Age-related increases in chronic systemic inflammation are strong predictors of morbidity and mortality in high income countries, but evidence is lacking from lower- and middle-income settings where infectious diseases are more prevalent and rates of overweight and obesity are relatively low. Here we evaluate two complementary measures of chronic inflammation—plasma C-reactive protein (CRP) and a DNA methylation–based surrogate (DNAm-CRP)—measured at baseline as predictors of physical capacity, cognitive function, and cardiometabolic disease seven years later among women in the Philippines (N = 953; 43-75 years at follow-up). Levels of CRP and DNAm-CRP were not strongly associated with age. Both measures predicted subsequent declines in physical and functional capacity, increased incidence of diabetes and hypertension, and poorer cognitive performance, after adjustment for baseline status and other covariates. DNAm-CRP performed comparably to CRP, and was robust to variation in white blood cell composition and acute infectious symptoms at the time of sampling. These findings demonstrate that chronic inflammation is associated with multiple dimensions of aging in a lower-middle income setting, and highlights the utility of inflammatory biomarkers as scalable tools for global aging research.

reviewRecords.title: Societal actors’ perceptions of intersectoral collaboration and the participation of older adults in the development of age-friendly environments
reviewRecords.abstract: Older adults’ participation and intersectoral collaboration are central to the development of age-friendly environments. While previous research has emphasised the importance of these principles, less is known about how they are understood and enacted by societal actors in practice. This creates a need to explore societal actors’ perceptions of both intersectoral collaboration and older adults’ participation in the development of age-friendly environments. Method The study had a participatory qualitative design. Data were collected through a World Café involving 19 societal actors in a Swedish municipal context. Participants represented several societal sectors relevant to age-friendly environments, including welfare, care, public health, governance, social sustainability, urban planning,mobility, civil society, and voluntary engagement. Findings The findings showed that participants perceived intersectoral collaboration as requiring shared societal responsibility across multiple sectors, while responsibility risked becoming unclear when no actor had an explicit mandate to coordinate, prioritise and act. Intersectoral collaboration was viewed as a way of sharing resources, yet also as vulnerable when it relied mainly on personal relationships and informal networks rather than organisationally embedded structures. Similarly, older adults’ participation was highly valued when developing age-friendly initiatives, but participants questioned whether existing participation channels adequately reflect the diversity of older adults’ experiences and needs.  Age-friendly work requires shared responsibility across societal actors, supported by clear coordination. Personal relationships and informal networks should be recognised as valuable for enabling collaboration, but they need to be complemented by formal structures to ensure sustainability over time. Moreover, greater efforts to reach seldom-heard older adults are needed. Doing so may contribute to more nuanced and age-friendly initiatives that better reflect the diverse needs of the older population.
